al-Zajjaj (Ibrahim ibn al-Sari al-Zajjaj) denied that the glorification of non-rational beings is the glorification of indication (dalala). He said: "If this were the glorification of indication and the manifestation of the traces of creation, it would be understood, so why did He say: ﴿but you do not understand their glorification﴾? Its original form is to be transitive by itself, because the meaning of "sabbahtuhu" is "I removed him far from evil." When it is used with lam, that lam is either extra for emphasis, as in "shakartuhu" and "shakartu lahu" (I thanked him), or it is for causation, meaning: perform the glorification for the sake of Allah, sincerely for Him, glorified be He. This verb occurs in some of the opening surahs in the past tense, as in this surah, in some in the present tense, and in some in the imperative, to indicate that these things glorify Allah at all times; their glorification is not restricted to one time rather than another, but they glorify Him forever, in the past, and they will glorify Him forever in the future.

﴿And He is the Almighty﴾, meaning: the All-Powerful, the Overpowering, whom no one contests and whom no one can prevent, whatever He may be; ﴿the All-Wise﴾, who does the acts of wisdom and rightness.

﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, He disposes of it alone, and no action other than His disposal and command takes effect. It has been said that He meant the treasures of rain, plants and all provisions. ﴿He gives life and causes death﴾: the two verbs are either in the place of raising (rafa') as predicates of an omitted subject, or in the place of accusative (nasb) as a circumstantial clause (hal) from a pronoun referring to Him, or it is a resumed statement explaining some rulings of dominion. The meaning is that He gives life in this world and causes the living to die. It has been said: He gives life to the drops of semen, which are lifeless, and causes the living to die. It has been said: He gives life to the dead for resurrection. ﴿And He is over all things competent﴾, nothing can overpower Him, whatever it may be.

﴿He is the First﴾ before everything, ﴿and the Last﴾ after everything, meaning the One who remains after the annihilation of His creation; ﴿the Outward﴾, the High, the Overpowering over everything; or the Outward, meaning His existence is manifest through clear proofs; ﴿and the Inward﴾, meaning the One who knows what is hidden, from the saying of people: "So-and-so conceals (yubtinu) the matter of so-and-so," meaning he knows the inner part of his affair. It may also mean: the One concealed from sights and minds. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained these four names, as will come, so it is necessary to refer to that. ﴿And He is, of all things, Knowing﴾, nothing of the known escapes His knowledge.

﴿He is the One who created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾: this is an explanation of part of His dominion over the heavens and the earth, and its explanation has already been given fully in Surat al-A'raf and elsewhere.

al-Zajjaj (Ibrahim ibn al-Sari al-Zajjaj) denied that the glorification of non-rational beings is the glorification of indication (dalala). He said: "If this were the glorification of indication and the manifestation of the traces of creation, it would be understood, so why did He say: ﴿but you do not understand their glorification﴾? Its original form is to be transitive by itself, because the meaning of "sabbahtuhu" is "I removed him far from evil." When it is used with lam, that lam is either extra for emphasis, as in "shakartuhu" and "shakartu lahu" (I thanked him), or it is for causation, meaning: perform the glorification for the sake of Allah, sincerely for Him, glorified be He. This verb occurs in some of the opening surahs in the past tense, as in this surah, in some in the present tense, and in some in the imperative, to indicate that these things glorify Allah at all times; their glorification is not restricted to one time rather than another, but they glorify Him forever, in the past, and they will glorify Him forever in the future.

It has been said that He meant the treasures of rain, plants and all provisions. ﴿He gives life and causes death﴾: the two verbs are either in the place of raising (rafa') as predicates of an omitted subject, or in the place of accusative (nasb) as a circumstantial clause (hal) from a pronoun referring to Him, or it is a resumed statement explaining some rulings of dominion. The meaning is that He gives life in this world and causes the living to die. It has been said: He gives life to the drops of semen, which are lifeless, and causes the living to die. It has been said: He gives life to the dead for resurrection. ﴿And He is over all things competent﴾, nothing can overpower Him, whatever it may be.

It may also mean: the One concealed from sights and minds. ﴿And He is the Almighty﴾, meaning: the All-Powerful, the Overpowering, whom no one contests and whom no one can prevent, whatever He may be; ﴿the All-Wise﴾, who does the acts of wisdom and rightness.

﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, He disposes of it alone, and no action other than His disposal and command takes effect. It has been said that He meant the treasures of rain, plants and all provisions. ﴿He gives life and causes death﴾: the two verbs are either in the place of raising (rafa') as predicates of an omitted subject, or in the place of accusative (nasb) as a circumstantial clause (hal) from a pronoun referring to Him, or it is a resumed statement explaining some rulings of dominion. The meaning is that He gives life in this world and causes the living to die. It has been said: He gives life to the drops of semen, which are lifeless, and causes the living to die. It has been said: He gives life to the dead for resurrection. ﴿And He is over all things competent﴾, nothing can overpower Him, whatever it may be.

﴿He is the First﴾ before everything, ﴿and the Last﴾ after everything, meaning the One who remains after the annihilation of His creation; ﴿the Outward﴾, the High, the Overpowering over everything; or the Outward, meaning His existence is manifest through clear proofs; ﴿and the Inward﴾, meaning the One who knows what is hidden, from the saying of people: "So-and-so conceals (yubtinu) the matter of so-and-so," meaning he knows the inner part of his affair. It may also mean: the One concealed from sights and minds. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained these four names, as will come, so it is necessary to refer to that. ﴿And He is, of all things, Knowing﴾, nothing of the known escapes His knowledge.

﴿He is the One who created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾: this is an explanation of part of His dominion over the heavens and the earth, and its explanation has already been given fully in Surat al-A'raf and elsewhere.

﴿He knows what enters into the earth﴾, meaning what goes into it of rain and other things; ﴿and what emerges from it﴾, of plants and other things; ﴿and what descends from the sky﴾, of rain and other things; ﴿and what ascends into it﴾, meaning what rises up to it of the angels and the deeds of the servants. The explanation of this has already been given in Surat Saba.

﴿And He is with you wherever you are﴾, meaning by His power, His authority and His knowledge. This is an image for encompassing whatever proceeds from them, wherever they move on the earth, by land or by sea. ﴿And Allah, of what you do, is Seeing﴾, nothing of your deeds is hidden from Him.

(p-١٤٥٥)﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾: this repetition is for emphasis. ﴿And to Allah are returned all matters﴾, not to other than Him.

The majority (al-Jumhur) recited ﴿تُرْجَعُ﴾ (turja'u, "are returned") in the passive voice.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Amir recited it in the active voice (turja'u with the subject being Allah, i.e., "He returns").

﴿He causes the night to enter into the day, and causes the day to enter into the night﴾: the explanation of this has already been given in Surat Al 'Imran and in other places. ﴿And He is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾, meaning the thoughts within the breasts and what they conceal; nothing of that is hidden from Him.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Hurayra that he said: "Fatima came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asking him for a servant, and he said: 'Say: O Allah, Lord of the seven heavens and Lord of the Mighty Throne, our Lord and the Lord of everything, who sent down the Torah, the Gospel and the Furqan, who splits the grain and the date-stone, I seek refuge in You from the evil of everything You hold by its forelock. You are the First, so there is nothing before You; You are the Last, so there is nothing after You; You are the Outward, so there is nothing above You; You are the Inward, so there is nothing beneath You. Settle our debt for us and enrich us from poverty.'"

Ahmad, Muslim and others narrated, from another route of the hadith of Abu Hurayra, a marfu' report like this with the four names and their explanation.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated in al-'Azama from Ibn Umar and Abu Sa'id, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "People will continue to ask about everything until they say: 'This is Allah; He existed before everything. But what existed before Allah?' If they say that to you, then say: 'He is the First before everything, and the Last after whom there is nothing, and He is the Outward above everything, and He is the Inward beneath everything, and He is, of all things, Knowing.'"

Abu Dawud narrated from Abu Zumayl, who said: "I asked Ibn Abbas: 'Something that I find in my breast...' He said: 'What is it?' I said: 'By Allah, I will not speak of it.' He said to me: 'Is it some doubt?' and he laughed, and said: 'No one escapes that.' He said: 'Until Allah revealed: ﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you, then ask those who recite the Scripture before you﴾ [Yunus: 94].'" He said: "And he said to me: 'When you find something in yourself, say: He is the First, the Last, the Outward and the Inward, and He is, of all things, Knowing.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And He is with you wherever you are﴾, that he said: "He is Knowing of you wherever you are."

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 57, verses 10–11:**

His saying ﴿Believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ means: affirm the Oneness of God and the truth of the Messenger. This is addressed to the disbelievers of the Arabs. It is also possible that it is addressed to everyone, and that the command to believe, as regards the Muslims, means persisting in it or increasing in it. Then, after commanding them to believe, He commanded them to spend in the way of Allah, saying: ﴿And spend of that in which He has made you successors﴾, meaning: He has made you successors in disposing of it, without your owning it in reality, for the wealth is the wealth of Allah, and the servants are the successors of Allah over His wealth, so it is incumbent upon them to spend it in what pleases Him. It has also been said: He made you successors of those who were before you, from whom you inherit, and it will pass to others after you who will inherit from you, so do not be stingy with it.

Al-Hasan and others said this. It contains encouragement to spend in good before it passes from them and goes to others. The apparent meaning of the verse is encouragement to spend in good and in what Allah is pleased with in general. It has also been said that it is specific to the obligatory zakat, but there is no basis for this specification. Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned the reward of whoever spends in the way of Allah, saying: ﴿So those who believed among you and spent will have a great reward﴾, meaning: those who combined belief in Allah and His Messenger with spending in the way of Allah will have a great reward, which is Paradise.

﴿And what is [wrong] with you that you do not believe in Allah﴾. This interrogation is for rebuke and reproach: that is, what excuse do you have, and what prevents you from believing?

The causes have been removed from you. ﴿Ma﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), ﴿lakum﴾ is its predicate (khabar), and ﴿la tu'minun﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿lakum﴾, and the governing element is what it contains of the meaning of settledness (al-istiqrar). It has also been said that the meaning is: what good do you have of reward in the Hereafter if you do not believe? The clause ﴿while the Messenger calls you to believe in your Lord﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿la tu'minun﴾, by interlocking (al-tadakhul), and ﴿li-tu'minu﴾ is connected to ﴿yad'ukum﴾: that is, he calls you to belief. The meaning is: what excuse do you have for abandoning belief when the Messenger calls you to it and draws your attention to it? The clause ﴿and He has already taken your covenant﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause from the doer of ﴿yad'ukum﴾, also by interlocking: that is, while Allah has already taken your covenant when He brought you out from the loins of your father Adam, or by the proofs He has set up for you which indicate the Oneness of God and the obligation of belief.

The majority of readers read ﴿wa-qad akhadha﴾ in the active voice, the doer being Allah, glory be to Him, since His mention has preceded.

Abu 'Amr read in the passive voice ﴿in kuntum mu'minin﴾, meaning: by what has been taken from you of the covenant, or by the proofs and evidences, or: if you are believers by some means among the means. This is among the greatest of its means and the clearest of its requirements.

﴿He is the One who sends down upon His servant clear verses﴾, meaning: manifest and evident. These are the Qur'anic verses. It has also been said they are miracles, and the Qur'an is the greatest of them. ﴿To bring you out from darkness into light﴾, meaning: that Allah may bring you out through those verses from the darknesses of polytheism into the light of belief; or that the Messenger may bring you out through those verses, or through the call. ﴿And indeed, Allah is to you Kind and Merciful﴾, meaning: He is greatly full of kindness and mercy, and their intensity is complete, in that He sent down His books and sent His messengers to guide His servants. There is no kindness or mercy more complete than this.

The interrogation in His saying ﴿And what is [wrong] with you that you do not spend in the way of Allah﴾ is for rebuke and reproach, and the discussion of its grammatical analysis (i'rab) is like the discussion of the grammatical analysis of His saying ﴿And what is [wrong] with you that you do not believe in Allah﴾. In this verse is evidence that the spending commanded in His saying ﴿and spend of that in which He has made you successors﴾ is spending in the way of Allah, as we have explained. The meaning is: what excuse do you have, and what thing prevents you from that? The original is ﴿an la tunfiqu﴾. It has also been said that ﴿an﴾ is superfluous. The clause ﴿and to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause from the doer of ﴿alla tunfiqu﴾, or from its object. The meaning is: what thing prevents you from spending in that manner, while everything in the heavens and the earth returns to Allah, glory be to Him, at the ending of the world, like the return of an inheritance to the heir, and nothing of it remains for them? This is more inclusive for rebuke and more complete for reproach, for the fact that those wealths leave their owners and become Allah's, and none of their owners remains, is stronger in requiring spending upon them than the fact that they belong to Allah in reality, while they are His successors in disposing of them.

Then He, glory be to Him, explained the virtue of those who preceded in spending in the way of Allah, saying: ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest﴾. It has been said that the intended conquest is the conquest of Mecca, and most of the exegetes said this.

Al-Sha'bi and al-Zuhri said: the conquest of Hudaybiyya.

Qatada said: there were two kinds of fighting, one of which is better than the other, and two kinds of spending, one of which is better than the other. Fighting and spending before the conquest of Mecca were better than fighting and spending after it. Muqatil and others said likewise.

There is an omission in the speech, and the estimate is: those who spent before the conquest and fought are not equal to those who spent after the conquest and fought. It was omitted because it is clear, and because of what comes afterward indicating it. Spending and fighting before the conquest were better than spending and fighting after it, because the people's need at that time was greater while they were fewer and weaker. The placement of spending before fighting is to signal the excellence of spending because of their need for it, for they used to give of themselves and did not find what they could give of wealth.

Giving of oneself is the highest degree of generosity. The reference in His saying ﴿those﴾ is to ﴿man﴾ in terms of its meaning. It is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿greater in rank than those who spent afterward and fought﴾, meaning: higher in station and loftier in rank than those who spent their wealth in the way of Allah after the conquest and fought alongside the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ʿAṭāʾ said: the degrees of Paradise differ, and those who spent before the conquest are in its most excellent.

Al-Zajjaj said: because the earlier ones suffered more hardship than those after them, and their insights were also more penetrating.

The Prophet (ﷺ) directed attention to this virtue in his saying, as is authentically reported from him: "If one of you were to spend the weight of Uhud in gold, he would not reach a mudd of one of them nor half of it." This is an address from him (ﷺ) to those who came later in companionship, as the occasion on which this hadith was narrated also indicates.

﴿And to each Allah has promised the best﴾, meaning: to each of the two groups Allah has promised the best reward, which is Paradise, with the difference in their ranks within it.

The majority read ﴿wa-kullan﴾ in the accusative, as an object of the verb that follows it. Ibn 'Amir read it in the nominative, as a topic (ibtida'), with the sentence after it as its predicate and a omitted pronoun referring back to it; or as a predicate of an omitted subject. A similar usage is the saying of the poet:

*Umm al-Khiyar has come to claim against me a sin, all of it, which I did not commit.*

﴿And Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾, nothing of that is hidden from Him.

Then He, glory be to Him, encouraged charity, saying: ﴿Who is it that would lend to Allah a goodly loan﴾, meaning: who is it that would spend his wealth in the way of Allah, for that is like lending to Him. The Arabs say of everyone who does a good deed that he has lent. Among that is the saying of the poet:

*When you are repaid a loan, repay it; for it is only the young man who repays, not the camel.*

Al-Kalbi said: a loan (qard) means charity; "goodly" means seeking reward with the heart, without reminder or harm.

Muqatil said: "goodly" means that his soul is pleased with it. The explanation of this verse has already been given in Surat al-Baqara.

﴿And He will multiply it for him﴾. Ibn 'Amir and Ibn Kathir read ﴿fa-yud'ifahu﴾ without the alif, except that Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub put the fa' in the accusative.

Nafi' and the people of Kufa and Basra read ﴿fa-yuda'ifahu﴾ with the alif and with the 'ayn lightened, except that 'Asim put the fa' in the accusative, and the rest put it in the nominative.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: the nominative is by coordination with ﴿yuqridu﴾ (lends), or by resumption (isti'naf); and the accusative is because the fa' is in answer to the interrogation.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi weakened the accusative, saying: because the question did not fall on the loan, but on the doer of the loan; the fa' only puts into the accusative a verb that is subordinated to a verb about which a question is asked. But this group interpreted it according to meaning, as if His saying ﴿Who is it that would lend to Allah﴾ were equivalent to: "Would anyone lend to Allah, so that He multiplies it for him?"

﴿And he will have a noble reward﴾, which is Paradise. The multiplying here is that a good deed is multiplied to ten like it, up to seven hundred fold, according to differences in circumstances, persons, and times.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il reported, through the chain of Zayd ibn Aslam, from 'Ata' ibn Yasar, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "We went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the year of Hudaybiyya, until when we were at 'Usfan, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'It is about to happen that a people will come who will belittle your deeds in comparison with their deeds.' We said: 'Who are they, O Messenger of Allah? Are they Quraysh?' He said: 'No, but they are the people of Yemen; they are more tender of heart and softer of hearts.' We said: 'Are they better than us, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'If one of them had a mountain of gold, he would not reach a mudd of one of you nor half of it, except that this is the distinction between us and the people.' ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest﴾, the verse..." Ibn Kathir said: this hadith is strange with this chain, and Ibn Jarir narrated it but did not mention Hudaybiyya in it.

Ahmad reported from Anas, who said: "There was a dispute between Khalid ibn al-Walid and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf. Khalid said to 'Abd al-Rahman: 'You are exalting yourselves over us because of days you preceded us in?' This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'Leave my companions alone. By Him in whose hand is my soul, if you were to spend the weight of Uhud or the weight of the mountains in gold, you would not reach their deeds.'" What is in the Sahih from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with the wording: "Do not revile my companions. By Him in whose hand is my soul, if one of you spent the weight of Uhud in gold, he would not reach a mudd of one of them nor half of it." In another wording: "would not reach a mudd of one of them nor half of it." This hadith was reported by al-Bukhari, Muslim and others, from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.

Ibn Abi Shayba reported from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "Do not revile the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), for the standing of one of them for an hour is better than the deed of one of you for his whole life."

Khalid said to 'Abd al-Rahman: 'You are exalting yourselves over us because of days you preceded us in?' This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'Leave my companions alone. By Him in whose hand is my soul, if you were to spend the weight of Uhud or the weight of the mountains in gold, you would not reach their deeds.'" What is in the Sahih from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with the wording: "Do not revile my companions. By Him in whose hand is my soul, if one of you spent the weight of Uhud in gold, he would not reach a mudd of one of them nor half of it." In another wording: "would not reach a mudd of one of them nor half of it." This hadith was reported by al-Bukhari, Muslim and others, from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.

Ibn Abi Shayba reported from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "Do not revile the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), for the standing of one of them for an hour is better than the deed of one of you for his whole life."

(p-1457) His saying: ﴿On the day you see the believing men and believing women﴾. The verb governing the adverb of time (al-zarf) is implied. It is either "remember" (udhkur), or "generous" (karim), or "He will multiply it" (fa-yuda'if-hu), or it is the verb governing "for them" (lahum), which is "being established" (al-istiqrar). The address is to everyone who is fit to receive it. His saying: ﴿their light runs before them﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object of "you see". Light (nur) is the radiance that is seen. ﴿And on their right hands﴾ refers to the Sirat on the Day of Resurrection, and it is their guide to Paradise.

Qatadah said: Indeed the believer is given a light that shines as far as from 'Adan to San'a', and among the believers there is one whose light illuminates only the place of his two feet.

al-Dahhak and Muqatil said: "and on their right hands" means their books, which were given to them. So their books are in their right hands, and their light is before them.

al-Farra' said: The "ba'" (bi) here means "fi", that is, "in their right hands", or it means "'an" (concerning).

al-Dahhak also said: Their light is their guidance, and "on their right hands" is their books. Ibn Jarir al-Tabari chose this view, meaning: their faith and their righteous deeds run before them, and in their right hands are the books of their deeds. The majority of readers recited bi-aymanihim, plural of yamin (right hand).

Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi and Abu Haywah read bi-iymanihim, with a kasra on the hamza, on the basis that the intended meaning of al-iman is the opposite of disbelief (kufr). It was also said that it means the Qur'an. The prepositional phrases in both places are in the accusative position as circumstantial clauses (hal) from "their light", meaning: being between their hands and on their right hands. ﴿Your glad tidings today: gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever.﴾ "Your glad tidings" (bushraykum) is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is "gardens", with an omitted modifier: "the entry into gardens". The sentence is the object of an implied speech verb: it is said to them, and the one who says this to them is the angels.

Makki said: al-Farra' permitted the accusative of "gardens" as a circumstantial clause, with "today" as the predicate of "your glad tidings". But this is very far-fetched.

﴿Abiding therein forever﴾ is a predicated circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah). The demonstrative in His saying "that" refers to the light and the glad tidings. It is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿it is the great triumph﴾, meaning its greatness cannot be measured, so that it is as if there is no triumph other than it, and nothing else is considered.

﴿On the day the hypocrite men and hypocrite women will say﴾: "the day" (yawm) is a substitute (badal) for the first "the day". It is permissible for the governing word for it to be "the great triumph". It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative governed by an implied verb, meaning: remember. ﴿To those who believed﴾: the lam here is for conveying the message, like its parallels.

The majority read "unzuruna" as a command, with the hamza connected and the dammah on the ẓa', from naẓar in the sense of waiting (intizar), meaning: wait for us. They say this when they see the believers being hurried to Paradise.

al-A'mash, Hamzah, and Yahya ibn Wathhab read it with a cut hamza and a kasra on the ẓa', from inẓar, meaning: give us time and inform us. It is said: anẓartuhu and istanẓartuhu, meaning: I gave him time and I asked him for time.

al-Farra' said: The Arabs say anẓirni, meaning: wait for me. He cited the verse of 'Amr ibn Kulthum:

"Abu Hind, do not hasten against us, and wait for us, and we will inform you of certainty."

It was also said that the meaning of "unzuruna" is: look at us, because when they look at them, the believers face them and they are illuminated by their light. ﴿We will borrow from your light﴾, meaning we will be illuminated by it. The qabas is a flame of fire or a lamp. When they said this, ﴿it was said: Return behind you﴾, meaning the believers or the angels said to them, rebuking and mocking them: return behind you to the place from which we took the light. ﴿Then seek light﴾, meaning seek light for yourselves there, for it is from there that light is borrowed. It was also said the meaning is: return to the world and seek the light by what we sought it with, namely faith and righteous deeds. It was also said they meant by "light" what lies behind them of darkness, mocking them.

﴿So a wall was set up between them with a gate﴾. The sur (wall) is the barrier between two things, and what is meant here is the barrier between Paradise and Hell, or between the people of Paradise and the people of Hell.

al-Kisa'i said: the ba' in ﴿bi-surin﴾ is superfluous.

Then He, glorified is He, described the said wall, saying: ﴿It has a gate, its inner side has mercy in it﴾, meaning the inner side of that wall, which is the side facing the people of Paradise, has mercy in it, and this is Paradise. Its outer side, which is the side facing the people of the Fire, ﴿and from before it is punishment﴾, meaning from its direction is the punishment of Hell. It was also said that the believers will overtake them and enter Paradise.

The hypocrites will be in punishment, with the wall between them. It was also said that the mercy within it is the light of the believers, and the punishment on its outer side is the darkness of the hypocrites.

When the wall was set up between the believers and the hypocrites, God, glorified is He, told of what the hypocrites said at that time, saying: ﴿They will call out to them: Were we not with you?﴾, meaning we were in agreement with you outwardly, praying with your prayers in your mosques, and acting by the deeds of Islam like you. The sentence is a fresh resumption (isti'nafiyyah), as if it were said: what did the hypocrites say after the wall was set up between them and the believers? He said: they call out to them. Then He, glorified is He, told of what the believers answered them, saying: ﴿They will say: Yes﴾, meaning you were with us outwardly. ﴿But you tempted yourselves﴾ by hypocrisy and concealing disbelief.

Mujahid said: you destroyed them by hypocrisy. It was also said by lusts and pleasures. ﴿And you waited﴾ for Muhammad (ﷺ) and those with him among the believers, for the misfortunes of time. It was also said you waited for repentance, and the first is preferable. ﴿And you doubted﴾, meaning you were in doubt about the matter of religion, and did not believe in what was revealed of the Qur'an nor in the manifest miracles. ﴿And false desires deceived you﴾, which include what you were in of waiting, and it was said it is the prolonging of hope, and it was said what they wished for of the weakness of the believers.

Qatadah said: "the desires" here is the deception of Satan. It was also said: the world. It was also said: their hope for forgiveness. All these things enter into the meaning of desires. ﴿Until the command of God came﴾, which is death. It was also said: His help to His Prophet (ﷺ).

Qatadah said: it is their being cast into the Fire. ﴿And the Deceiver deceived you about God﴾. The majority read "al-Ghurur" with a fatha on the ghayn, which is an adjective on the pattern fa'ul, and what is meant by it is Satan, meaning: he deceived you through God's forbearance and His respite to Satan.

Abu Haywah, Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa', and Simak ibn Harb read it with a dammah, and it is a verbal noun (masdar).

﴿So today no ransom will be taken from you﴾, by which you might ransom your souls from the Fire, O hypocrites, ﴿nor from those who disbelieved﴾ in God, outwardly and inwardly. ﴿Your abode is the Fire﴾, meaning your dwelling place to which you retreat is the Fire. ﴿It is your master﴾, meaning it has more right over you. The word mawla originally means one who takes care of a person's affairs, then it was used for one who stays close to him. It was also said the meaning of "your mawla" is: your place, from near, from the walī, which is the one close by.

It was also said that God places life and reason into the Fire, so it is distinguished by fury against the disbelievers. It was also said the meaning is: it is your helper, following the line of the poet's verse:

"Their greeting among them is a painful striking."

﴿And wretched is the destination﴾, to which you go, which is the Fire.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, have transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud concerning ﴿their light runs before them﴾ that he said: their light is given to them according to the measure of their deeds as they cross the Sirat. Among them is one whose light is like a mountain, and among them one whose light is like a palm tree, and the least of them in light is one whose light is on his big toe; it goes out once and is kindled another time.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: While people were in darkness, God sent forth a light. When the believers saw the light they turned toward it, and the light was their guide from God to Paradise. When the hypocrites saw the believers setting off toward the light, they followed them, so God made darkness fall upon the hypocrites, and then they said: ﴿Wait for us, that we may borrow from your light﴾, for we were with you in the world. The believers said: ﴿Return behind you﴾, from where you came, from the darkness, ﴿then seek﴾ light there.

al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from him, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God calls people on the Day of Resurrection by their mothers, as a veil from Him over His servants. But at the Sirat, God gives every believer a light and every hypocrite a light. When they stand upon the Sirat, God takes away the light of the hypocrite men and the hypocrite women, and the hypocrites say: ﴿Wait for us, that we may borrow from your light﴾, and the believers say: ﴿Our Lord, complete for us our light﴾. At that time no one will remember anyone else." There are other hadiths and reports on this subject.

'Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit that he was on the wall of Bayt al-Maqdis and wept. He was asked what made him weep, and he said: Here the Messenger of God (ﷺ) told us that he saw Hell.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn 'Asakir transmitted from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, who said: The wall that God mentioned in the Qur'an, ﴿So a wall was set up between them with a gate﴾, is the wall which is in the eastern part of Bayt al-Maqdis. ﴿Its inner side has mercy in it﴾ is the mosque, and ﴿its outer side, from before it is punishment﴾ means the valley of Hell and what is adjacent to it.

It is not hidden from you that the interpretation of the wall mentioned in the Qur'an in this verse as this wall which is in Bayt al-Maqdis contains difficulties that no argument can remove, especially after the addition of the words "its inner side has mercy in it" as the mosque. For this is not what the verse was brought for, nor what it indicates. Where is Bayt al-Maqdis or its wall in relation to the wall dividing the two groups of believers and hypocrites? And what sense is there in mentioning the mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis here? If what is meant is that God removes the wall of Bayt al-Maqdis and makes it in the Hereafter a wall set between the believers and the hypocrites, then what is the sense of interpreting the inner side of the wall and what is in it of mercy as the mosque? And if what is meant is that God drives both groups, the believers and the hypocrites, to Bayt al-Maqdis, and makes the believers inside the walls in the mosque and makes the hypocrites outside it, then they are at that time on the Sirat and on the way to Paradise, and they are not in Bayt al-Maqdis. So if such an interpretation is established from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), we accept it and believe in it; otherwise there is no honour nor acceptance for it.

﴿On the day the hypocrite men and hypocrite women will say﴾: "the day" (yawm) is a substitute (badal) for the first "the day". It is permissible for the governing word for it to be "the great triumph". It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative governed by an implied verb, meaning: remember. ﴿To those who believed﴾: the lam here is for conveying the message, like its parallels.

The majority read "unzuruna" as a command, with the hamza connected and the dammah on the ẓa', from naẓar in the sense of waiting (intizar), meaning: wait for us. They say this when they see the believers being hurried to Paradise.

al-A'mash, Hamzah, and Yahya ibn Wathhab read it with a cut hamza and a kasra on the ẓa', from inẓar, meaning: give us time and inform us. It is said: anẓartuhu and istanẓartuhu, meaning: I gave him time and I asked him for time.

al-Farra' said: The Arabs say anẓirni, meaning: wait for me. He cited the verse of 'Amr ibn Kulthum:

"Abu Hind, do not hasten against us, and wait for us, and we will inform you of certainty."

It was also said that the meaning of "unzuruna" is: look at us, because when they look at them, the believers face them and they are illuminated by their light. ﴿We will borrow from your light﴾, meaning we will be illuminated by it. The qabas is a flame of fire or a lamp. When they said this, ﴿it was said: Return behind you﴾, meaning the believers or the angels said to them, rebuking and mocking them: return behind you to the place from which we took the light. ﴿Then seek light﴾, meaning seek light for yourselves there, for it is from there that light is borrowed. It was also said the meaning is: return to the world and seek the light by what we sought it with, namely faith and righteous deeds. It was also said they meant by "light" what lies behind them of darkness, mocking them.

﴿So a wall was set up between them with a gate﴾. The sur (wall) is the barrier between two things, and what is meant here is the barrier between Paradise and Hell, or between the people of Paradise and the people of Hell.

al-Kisa'i said: the ba' in ﴿bi-surin﴾ is superfluous.

Then He, glorified is He, described the said wall, saying: ﴿It has a gate, its inner side has mercy in it﴾, meaning the inner side of that wall, which is the side facing the people of Paradise, has mercy in it, and this is Paradise. Its outer side, which is the side facing the people of the Fire, ﴿and from before it is punishment﴾, meaning from its direction is the punishment of Hell. It was also said that the believers will overtake them and enter Paradise.

The hypocrites will be in punishment, with the wall between them. It was also said that the mercy within it is the light of the believers, and the punishment on its outer side is the darkness of the hypocrites.

When the wall was set up between the believers and the hypocrites, God, glorified is He, told of what the hypocrites said at that time, saying: ﴿They will call out to them: Were we not with you?﴾, meaning we were in agreement with you outwardly, praying with your prayers in your mosques, and acting by the deeds of Islam like you. The sentence is a fresh resumption (isti'nafiyyah), as if it were said: what did the hypocrites say after the wall was set up between them and the believers? He said: they call out to them. Then He, glorified is He, told of what the believers answered them, saying: ﴿They will say: Yes﴾, meaning you were with us outwardly. ﴿But you tempted yourselves﴾ by hypocrisy and concealing disbelief.

Mujahid said: you destroyed them by hypocrisy. It was also said by lusts and pleasures. ﴿And you waited﴾ for Muhammad (ﷺ) and those with him among the believers, for the misfortunes of time. It was also said you waited for repentance, and the first is preferable. ﴿And you doubted﴾, meaning you were in doubt about the matter of religion, and did not believe in what was revealed of the Qur'an nor in the manifest miracles. ﴿And false desires deceived you﴾, which include what you were in of waiting, and it was said it is the prolonging of hope, and it was said what they wished for of the weakness of the believers.

Qatadah said: "the desires" here is the deception of Satan. It was also said: the world. It was also said: their hope for forgiveness. All these things enter into the meaning of desires. ﴿Until the command of God came﴾, which is death. It was also said: His help to His Prophet (ﷺ).

Qatadah said: it is their being cast into the Fire. ﴿And the Deceiver deceived you about God﴾. The majority read "al-Ghurur" with a fatha on the ghayn, which is an adjective on the pattern fa'ul, and what is meant by it is Satan, meaning: he deceived you through God's forbearance and His respite to Satan.

Abu Haywah, Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa', and Simak ibn Harb read it with a dammah, and it is a verbal noun (masdar).

﴿So today no ransom will be taken from you﴾, by which you might ransom your souls from the Fire, O hypocrites, ﴿nor from those who disbelieved﴾ in God, outwardly and inwardly. ﴿Your abode is the Fire﴾, meaning your dwelling place to which you retreat is the Fire. ﴿It is your master﴾, meaning it has more right over you. The word mawla originally means one who takes care of a person's affairs, then it was used for one who stays close to him. It was also said the meaning of "your mawla" is: your place, from near, from the walī, which is the one close by.

It was also said that God places life and reason into the Fire, so it is distinguished by fury against the disbelievers. It was also said the meaning is: it is your helper, following the line of the poet's verse:

"Their greeting among them is a painful striking."

﴿And wretched is the destination﴾, to which you go, which is the Fire.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, have transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud concerning ﴿their light runs before them﴾ that he said: their light is given to them according to the measure of their deeds as they cross the Sirat. Among them is one whose light is like a mountain, and among them one whose light is like a palm tree, and the least of them in light is one whose light is on his big toe; it goes out once and is kindled another time.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: While people were in darkness, God sent forth a light. When the believers saw the light they turned toward it, and the light was their guide from God to Paradise. When the hypocrites saw the believers setting off toward the light, they followed them, so God made darkness fall upon the hypocrites, and then they said: ﴿Wait for us, that we may borrow from your light﴾, for we were with you in the world. The believers said: ﴿Return behind you﴾, from where you came, from the darkness, ﴿then seek﴾ light there.

al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from him, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God calls people on the Day of Resurrection by their mothers, as a veil from Him over His servants. But at the Sirat, God gives every believer a light and every hypocrite a light. When they stand upon the Sirat, God takes away the light of the hypocrite men and the hypocrite women, and the hypocrites say: ﴿Wait for us, that we may borrow from your light﴾, and the believers say: ﴿Our Lord, complete for us our light﴾. At that time no one will remember anyone else." There are other hadiths and reports on this subject.

'Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit that he was on the wall of Bayt al-Maqdis and wept. He was asked what made him weep, and he said: Here the Messenger of God (ﷺ) told us that he saw Hell.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn 'Asakir transmitted from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, who said: The wall that God mentioned in the Qur'an, ﴿So a wall was set up between them with a gate﴾, is the wall which is in the eastern part of Bayt al-Maqdis. ﴿Its inner side has mercy in it﴾ is the mosque, and ﴿its outer side, from before it is punishment﴾ means the valley of Hell and what is adjacent to it.

It is not hidden from you that the interpretation of the wall mentioned in the Qur'an in this verse as this wall which is in Bayt al-Maqdis contains difficulties that no argument can remove, especially after the addition of the words "its inner side has mercy in it" as the mosque. For this is not what the verse was brought for, nor what it indicates. Where is Bayt al-Maqdis or its wall in relation to the wall dividing the two groups of believers and hypocrites? And what sense is there in mentioning the mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis here? If what is meant is that God removes the wall of Bayt al-Maqdis and makes it in the Hereafter a wall set between the believers and the hypocrites, then what is the sense of interpreting the inner side of the wall and what is in it of mercy as the mosque? And if what is meant is that God drives both groups, the believers and the hypocrites, to Bayt al-Maqdis, and makes the believers inside the walls in the mosque and makes the hypocrites outside it, then they are at that time on the Sirat and on the way to Paradise, and they are not in Bayt al-Maqdis. So if such an interpretation is established from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), we accept it and believe in it; otherwise there is no honour nor acceptance for it.

al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿But you tempted yourselves﴾, he said: by lusts and pleasures. ﴿And you waited﴾, he said: for repentance. ﴿And false desires deceived you until the command of God came﴾, he said: death. ﴿And the Deceiver deceived you about God﴾, he said: Satan.

(p-1457) His saying: ﴿On the day you see the believing men and believing women﴾. The verb governing the adverb of time (al-zarf) is implied. It is either "remember" (udhkur), or "generous" (karim), or "He will multiply it" (fa-yuda'if-hu), or it is the verb governing "for them" (lahum), which is "being established" (al-istiqrar). The address is to everyone who is fit to receive it. His saying: ﴿their light runs before them﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object of "you see". Light (nur) is the radiance that is seen. ﴿And on their right hands﴾ refers to the Sirat on the Day of Resurrection, and it is their guide to Paradise.

Qatadah said: Indeed the believer is given a light that shines as far as from 'Adan to San'a', and among the believers there is one whose light illuminates only the place of his two feet.

al-Dahhak and Muqatil said: "and on their right hands" means their books, which were given to them. So their books are in their right hands, and their light is before them.

al-Farra' said: The "ba'" (bi) here means "fi", that is, "in their right hands", or it means "'an" (concerning).

al-Dahhak also said: Their light is their guidance, and "on their right hands" is their books. Ibn Jarir al-Tabari chose this view, meaning: their faith and their righteous deeds run before them, and in their right hands are the books of their deeds. The majority of readers recited bi-aymanihim, plural of yamin (right hand).

Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi and Abu Haywah read bi-iymanihim, with a kasra on the hamza, on the basis that the intended meaning of al-iman is the opposite of disbelief (kufr). It was also said that it means the Qur'an. The prepositional phrases in both places are in the accusative position as circumstantial clauses (hal) from "their light", meaning: being between their hands and on their right hands. ﴿Your glad tidings today: gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever.﴾ "Your glad tidings" (bushraykum) is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is "gardens", with an omitted modifier: "the entry into gardens". The sentence is the object of an implied speech verb: it is said to them, and the one who says this to them is the angels.

Makki said: al-Farra' permitted the accusative of "gardens" as a circumstantial clause, with "today" as the predicate of "your glad tidings". But this is very far-fetched.

His saying: ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe﴾. It is said: *anā laka yaʾnī anan* (أنى لك يأني أنى), meaning "when it has drawn near" (إذا حان).

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿ألَمْ يَأْنِ﴾, but al-Hasan and Abu al-Simak read "ألَمّا يَأْنِ". Ibn al-Sikkit recited:

*Has it not yet come for me that my blindness be cleared,*
*and that I refrain from Layla? Indeed, it has drawn near for me.*

And ﴿that their hearts should humble themselves﴾ is the subject (fāʿil) of *yaʾnī*, meaning: has the humbling of their hearts not arrived, and its time not come? From this is the saying of the poet:

*Has it not come for me, O heart, that I abandon ignorance,*
*and that gray hair, shining, should give us intellect?*

This verse was revealed concerning the believers.

Al-Hasan said: He is slow to them, though they are the most beloved of His creation to Him.

It was also said that the address is to those who believed in Moses and Jesus, not in Muhammad (ﷺ).

Al-Zajjaj said: It was revealed concerning a group of the believers who were urged to tenderness and humility. As for those whom Allah described as tender and humble, they are a class above these.

Al-Suddi and others said: The meaning is: has the time not come for those who believe outwardly, while concealing disbelief, that their hearts should humble themselves ﴿to the remembrance of Allah﴾. What will come at the end of this discussion strengthens the view of those who said it was revealed concerning the Muslims. Humility (khushūʿ) is softness and tenderness of the heart.

The meaning is that the remembrance should bring them humility and tenderness, and that they should not be like those whose hearts do not soften to the remembrance and do not humble themselves before it. ﴿And what has come down of the truth﴾ is conjoined to "the remembrance of Allah." The "truth that has come down" is the Qur'an. The remembrance conjoined to it is then understood as anything else in which Allah the Glorified is mentioned by the tongue or by the heart's recollection. It was also said that the "remembrance" is the Qur'an itself, in which case this conjunction is of the type of explanatory conjunction (ʿaṭf al-tafsīr), or it is considered by the difference in the two concepts.

The majority read *nazala* (نَزَلَ) with shadda, in the active voice. Nafiʿ and Hafs read it with light pronunciation, in the active voice. Ibn Masʿud read *unzila* (أُنْزِلَ), in the passive voice.

﴿And that they should not be like those who were given the Book before⟩: The majority read it with the yāʾ (third person), following what preceded. Abu Ḥaywa and Ibn Abi ʿAbla read it with the tāʾ (second person), as a shift (iltifāt) to address, and Ibn Isḥaq and ʿĪsā also read it so. The clause is conjoined to *takhsaʿa*: that is, has the time not come for them that their hearts should humble themselves, and that they should not be…? The meaning is a prohibition on them from following the path of the Jews and Christians who were given the Torah and the Gospel before the revelation of the Qur'an.

﴿So the term grew long for them⟩, i.e., the time lengthened between them and their prophets.

The majority read *al-amad* (الأمَدُ) with a light dāl. Ibn Kathir, in one transmission from him, read it with shadda: meaning the long time. It was said that on the first reading *al-amad* means the term and the end point, as one says "amad fulān kadhā," meaning his limit.

﴿So their hearts became hard﴾ because of that cause, and so they distorted and altered. Allah the Glorified forbade the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) to be like them.

﴿And many of them are defiant⟩, i.e., outside obedience to Allah, because they abandoned acting upon what was revealed to them, distorted and altered, and did not believe in what was sent down to Muhammad (ﷺ). It was said that they are those who abandoned belief in Jesus and Muhammad (ﷺ). It was said that they are those who innovated monasticism, the people of the monasteries.

﴿Know that Allah gives life to the earth after its death﴾: He is therefore able to resurrect bodies after their death, and to soften hearts after their hardness. ﴿We have indeed made clear to you the signs﴾, among which are these verses, ﴿so that you may understand⟩, i.e., that you may understand what they contain of admonitions and act according to their requirement.

﴿Indeed, the male and female givers of charity⟩: The majority read it with shadda on the *ṣād* in both places, from *ṣadaqa* (charity). The original is *al-mutaṣaddiqīn* and *al-mutaṣaddiqāt*, and the tāʾ was assimilated into the ṣād. Ubayy read *al-mutaṣaddiqīn* and *al-mutaṣaddiqāt* with the tāʾ retained, in accordance with the original. Ibn Kathir read with a light ṣād in both places, from *taṣdīq* (belief): that is, they affirmed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in what he brought.

﴿And who lend to Allah a goodly loan﴾ is conjoined to the active participle in *al-muṣṣaddiqīn*, because when it came as the relative clause (ṣila) of the definite article *alif-lām*, it took the place of a verb. So it is as if it said: "Indeed, those who give charity and lend such-and-such." This is the view of Abu ʿAli al-Farisi and others.

It was said that the clause *wa-aqraḍū* is parenthetical between the subject of *inna* and its predicate, which is *yuḍāʿafu*. It was also said that it is the relative clause of an omitted relative pronoun, i.e., "and those who lend." The "goodly loan" is an expression for charity and spending in the way of Allah, together with sincerity of intention, correctness of purpose, and seeking reward.

The majority read ﴿yuḍāʿafu lahum﴾ with a fatha on the ʿayn, in the passive voice. The element standing in for the subject is either the prepositional phrase, or a pronoun referring to *al-muṣṣaddiqīn* with an omitted noun: that is, their reward. Al-Aʿmash read *yuḍāʿifuhu* with a kasra on the ʿayn and an added hāʾ.

Abu Yaʿla and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him also, who said: "When this verse was revealed, some of us turned to others saying: 'What have we newly done? What have we done?'"

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Allah found the hearts of the emigrants slow, so He rebuked them at the close of thirteen years from the revelation of the Qur'an: ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe…﴾ the verse."

Ibn Abi Shayba in *al-Musannaf* narrated from ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn Abi Rawwad that the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) had developed jesting and laughter, so this verse was revealed: ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe…﴾.

Ibn al-Mubarak narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿Know that Allah gives life to the earth after its death﴾ that he said: "It means that He softens the hearts after their hardness."

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Bara ibn ʿAzib, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'The believers of my community are martyrs.' Then the Prophet (ﷺ) recited: ﴿And those who believe in Allah and His messengers, those are the truthful and the martyrs with their Lord﴾."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Masʿud, who said: "Every believer is truthful and a martyr."

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn Masʿud, who said: "Indeed a man may die upon his bed while he is a martyr," then he recited this verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated similar from Abu Hurayra.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿And those who believe in Allah and His messengers, those are the truthful﴾ that he said: "This is a separate sentence, and then ﴿and the martyrs, with their Lord, for them is their reward and their light﴾."

Ibn Hibban narrated from ʿAmr ibn Murra al-Juhani, who said: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what do you say if I testify that there is no god but Allah and that you are the Messenger of Allah, pray the five prayers, pay zakat, fast Ramadan and stand in its night prayer? Then with whom am I?' He said: 'With the truthful and the martyrs.'"

His saying: ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe﴾. It is said: *anā laka yaʾnī anan* (أنى لك يأني أنى), meaning "when it has drawn near" (إذا حان).

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿ألَمْ يَأْنِ﴾, but al-Hasan and Abu al-Simak read "ألَمّا يَأْنِ". Ibn al-Sikkit recited:

*Has it not yet come for me that my blindness be cleared,*
*and that I refrain from Layla? Indeed, it has drawn near for me.*

And ﴿that their hearts should humble themselves﴾ is the subject (fāʿil) of *yaʾnī*, meaning: has the humbling of their hearts not arrived, and its time not come? From this is the saying of the poet:

*Has it not come for me, O heart, that I abandon ignorance,*
*and that gray hair, shining, should give us intellect?*

This verse was revealed concerning the believers.

Al-Hasan said: He is slow to them, though they are the most beloved of His creation to Him.

It was also said that the address is to those who believed in Moses and Jesus, not in Muhammad (ﷺ).

Al-Zajjaj said: It was revealed concerning a group of the believers who were urged to tenderness and humility. As for those whom Allah described as tender and humble, they are a class above these.

Al-Suddi and others said: The meaning is: has the time not come for those who believe outwardly, while concealing disbelief, that their hearts should humble themselves ﴿to the remembrance of Allah﴾. What will come at the end of this discussion strengthens the view of those who said it was revealed concerning the Muslims. Humility (khushūʿ) is softness and tenderness of the heart.

The meaning is that the remembrance should bring them humility and tenderness, and that they should not be like those whose hearts do not soften to the remembrance and do not humble themselves before it. ﴿And what has come down of the truth﴾ is conjoined to "the remembrance of Allah." The "truth that has come down" is the Qur'an. The remembrance conjoined to it is then understood as anything else in which Allah the Glorified is mentioned by the tongue or by the heart's recollection. It was also said that the "remembrance" is the Qur'an itself, in which case this conjunction is of the type of explanatory conjunction (ʿaṭf al-tafsīr), or it is considered by the difference in the two concepts.

The majority read *nazala* (نَزَلَ) with shadda, in the active voice. Nafiʿ and Hafs read it with light pronunciation, in the active voice. Ibn Masʿud read *unzila* (أُنْزِلَ), in the passive voice.

﴿And that they should not be like those who were given the Book before⟩: The majority read it with the yāʾ (third person), following what preceded. Abu Ḥaywa and Ibn Abi ʿAbla read it with the tāʾ (second person), as a shift (iltifāt) to address, and Ibn Isḥaq and ʿĪsā also read it so. The clause is conjoined to *takhsaʿa*: that is, has the time not come for them that their hearts should humble themselves, and that they should not be…? The meaning is a prohibition on them from following the path of the Jews and Christians who were given the Torah and the Gospel before the revelation of the Qur'an.

﴿So the term grew long for them⟩, i.e., the time lengthened between them and their prophets.

The majority read *al-amad* (الأمَدُ) with a light dāl. Ibn Kathir, in one transmission from him, read it with shadda: meaning the long time. It was said that on the first reading *al-amad* means the term and the end point, as one says "amad fulān kadhā," meaning his limit.

﴿So their hearts became hard﴾ because of that cause, and so they distorted and altered. Allah the Glorified forbade the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) to be like them.

﴿And many of them are defiant⟩, i.e., outside obedience to Allah, because they abandoned acting upon what was revealed to them, distorted and altered, and did not believe in what was sent down to Muhammad (ﷺ). It was said that they are those who abandoned belief in Jesus and Muhammad (ﷺ). It was said that they are those who innovated monasticism, the people of the monasteries.

﴿Know that Allah gives life to the earth after its death﴾: He is therefore able to resurrect bodies after their death, and to soften hearts after their hardness. ﴿We have indeed made clear to you the signs﴾, among which are these verses, ﴿so that you may understand⟩, i.e., that you may understand what they contain of admonitions and act according to their requirement.

﴿Indeed, the male and female givers of charity⟩: The majority read it with shadda on the *ṣād* in both places, from *ṣadaqa* (charity). The original is *al-mutaṣaddiqīn* and *al-mutaṣaddiqāt*, and the tāʾ was assimilated into the ṣād. Ubayy read *al-mutaṣaddiqīn* and *al-mutaṣaddiqāt* with the tāʾ retained, in accordance with the original. Ibn Kathir read with a light ṣād in both places, from *taṣdīq* (belief): that is, they affirmed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in what he brought.

﴿And who lend to Allah a goodly loan﴾ is conjoined to the active participle in *al-muṣṣaddiqīn*, because when it came as the relative clause (ṣila) of the definite article *alif-lām*, it took the place of a verb. So it is as if it said: "Indeed, those who give charity and lend such-and-such." This is the view of Abu ʿAli al-Farisi and others.

It was said that the clause *wa-aqraḍū* is parenthetical between the subject of *inna* and its predicate, which is *yuḍāʿafu*. It was also said that it is the relative clause of an omitted relative pronoun, i.e., "and those who lend." The "goodly loan" is an expression for charity and spending in the way of Allah, together with sincerity of intention, correctness of purpose, and seeking reward.

The majority read ﴿yuḍāʿafu lahum﴾ with a fatha on the ʿayn, in the passive voice. The element standing in for the subject is either the prepositional phrase, or a pronoun referring to *al-muṣṣaddiqīn* with an omitted noun: that is, their reward. Al-Aʿmash read *yuḍāʿifuhu* with a kasra on the ʿayn and an added hāʾ.

Ibn Kathir, Ibn ʿAmir, and Yaʿqub read *yuḍaʿʿafu* with shadda on the ʿayn and a fatha.

﴿And they will have a generous reward⟩, which is Paradise. The multiplication here is that a good deed is multiplied tenfold up to seven hundredfold.

﴿And those who believe in Allah and His messengers﴾, all of them. The demonstrative in His saying ﴿those﴾ refers to the relative noun. Its predicate is His saying ﴿they are the truthful and the martyrs﴾, and the sentence is the predicate of the relative noun.

Mujahid said: Everyone who believes in Allah and His messengers is a *ṣiddīq* (truthful one).

The two Muqatils said: They are those who did not doubt the messengers when those messengers informed them, and did not deny them.

Mujahid also said: This verse is specifically for the martyrs (shuhadāʾ), who are the prophets who bear witness for their nations and against them. Al-Farraʾ and al-Zajjaj chose this view.

Muqatil ibn Sulayman said: They are those who were martyred in the way of Allah, and so said Ibn Jarir. It was also said that they are the nations of the messengers, who bear witness on the Day of Resurrection for their prophets by their conveyance (of the message). The apparent meaning of the verse is: those who believe in Allah and His messengers, all of them, are in the rank of the truthful and the martyrs, the well-known ones with high standing before Allah. It was also said that the truthful ones are those who go to the utmost in truthfulness, in that they believed in Allah and affirmed all His messengers, and who stand for Allah the Glorified in monotheism.

Then the Glorified explained what good they have because of what they are characterized by, namely belief in Allah and His messengers, saying: ﴿For them is their reward and their light﴾. The first pronoun refers to the relative noun, and the last two pronouns refer to the truthful and the martyrs. So all three pronouns refer to one thing. The meaning is: for them is the reward and the light that were promised to them.

Then, having mentioned the state and reward of the believers, He mentioned the state and punishment of the disbelievers, saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs﴾, i.e., they combined disbelief with denial of the signs. The demonstrative *ulāʾika* refers to the relative noun in view of what its relative clause says of their being characterized by disbelief and denial. This is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿the companions of the blazing fire﴾. They will be tormented by it, and there is no reward for them and no light, but rather a lasting punishment and perpetual darkness.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Allah found the hearts of the emigrants slow, after seventeen years from the revelation of the Qur'an, so Allah revealed: ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe…﴾ the verse."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from ʿĀʾisha, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out to a group of his companions in the mosque while they were laughing. He dragged his cloak, his face reddened, and said: 'Do you laugh while there has not come to you an assurance from your Lord that He has forgiven you? Indeed He revealed upon me a verse concerning your laughter: ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves to the remembrance of Allah﴾.' They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what is the expiation of that?' He said: 'You weep as much as you laughed.'"

Muslim, al-Nasaʾi, Ibn Majah, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Masʿud, who said: "The time between our accepting Islam and Allah rebuking us with this verse, ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe…﴾, was only four years."

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh from another route, narrated similar from him.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 57, verses 20–24:

His saying, ﴿Know that the life of this world is but play and amusement﴾. When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the state of the second group, and what occurred from them of disbelief and denial, this being because of their inclination towards the world and its influence, He made clear its worthlessness and that it is too base to be preferred over the Last Abode. Al-la‘ib (play) is falsehood, and al-lahw (amusement) is everything one diverts oneself with and then it goes away.

Qatadah said: "Play and amusement: eating and drinking."

Mujahid said: "Every play is amusement." It was also said: al-la‘ib is that which inclines one to the world, and al-lahw is that which distracts one from the Hereafter and occupies one away from it. It was also said: al-la‘ib is acquisition (iqtina’), and al-lahw is women. The verification of this has already been discussed in Surat al-An‘am. Al-zinah (adornment) is adorning oneself with the goods of this world without action for the Hereafter. ﴿And boasting among you﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read tafakhur with tanwin, and the adverbial phrase is an attribute of it, or an object of it. Al-Sulami read it with idafah: that is, one of you boasts of it over another. It was said: they boast of physical form and strength, and it was said: of lineages and noble descent, as the Arabs used to do. ﴿And competition in wealth and children﴾, that is, they vie with one another in their wealth and children and exalt themselves through that over the poor.

Then, glory be to Him, made for this account a likeness and coined for it an example, so He said: ﴿like the example of rain whose vegetation pleases the disbelievers﴾, that is, like the example of rain whose vegetation pleases the farmers. What is meant by "the disbelievers" here is the farmers, because they cover (yakfuruna) the seed, that is, they cover it with soil. The meaning of "its vegetation" is the plant produced by it. ﴿Then it dries up﴾, that is, it withers after its greenness and dries out. ﴿So you see it turning yellow﴾, that is, changed from what it was of greenness; the brightness has turned to a yellow colour and wilting. ﴿Then it becomes debris﴾, that is, crumbled fragments, broken and shattered after its drying. The interpretation of this parable has already been given in Surat Yunus and al-Kahf. The meaning is that the life of this world is like a crop which pleases those who look at it because of its greenness and abundant freshness.

Then it is not long before it becomes stubble, chaff, as though it had never been.

It is also read as musfarran, and the kaf is in a place of nasb as a circumstantial (hal), or in a place of raf‘ as being a predicate after a predicate, or the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada').

Then, when He, glory be to Him, mentioned the worthlessness of the world and the swiftness of its passing, He mentioned what He has prepared for the disobedient in the Hereafter, so He said: ﴿And in the Hereafter there is severe punishment﴾, and He followed it with what He has prepared for the people of obedience, so He said: ﴿and forgiveness from Allah and approval﴾. The indefiniteness in both is for magnification.

Qatadah said: "Severe punishment is for the enemies of Allah. And forgiveness from Allah and approval is for His friends and the people of His obedience."

Al-Farra' said: The estimation in the verse is either "severe punishment" or "forgiveness," so one does not stop at "severe."

Then, after intimidation and encouragement, He, glory be to Him, mentioned the worthlessness of the world, so He said: ﴿And the life of this world is nothing but the goods of delusion﴾ for one who is deceived by it and does not work for his Hereafter.

Sa‘id ibn Jubayr said: "The goods of delusion are for one who does not occupy himself with seeking the Hereafter; and whoever occupies himself with seeking it, for him is the provision (mata‘ balagh) to what is better than it."

This sentence confirms and emphasises the preceding parable.

Then He urged His servants to race towards what necessitates forgiveness, namely repentance and righteous deeds, for that is a means to Paradise, so He said: ﴿Race towards forgiveness from your Lord﴾, that is, hasten with the haste of those who race, through righteous deeds which necessitate forgiveness for you from your Lord, and repent from what has occurred from you of sins. It was said that the intended meaning of the verse is the first takbir with the imam, as said by Makhul; and it was said the intended meaning is the first row.

There is no basis for restricting what is in the verse to such a thing; rather it is among what it applies to, either comprehensively or by way of substitution. ﴿And a Garden whose width is like the width of the heaven and earth﴾, that is, like their width. And if this is its measure in width, then what do you suppose of its length?

Al-Hasan said: "It means all the heavens and earths spread out, each one reaching to its companion." It was also said that the Garden whose width is this width is the garden of each one of the people of Paradise.

Ibn Kaysan said: "By it is meant one single garden of the gardens, and width is less than length. It is a habit of the Arabs to express a thing by its width without its length." Among this is the saying of the poet:

"As if the lands of Allah, though wide, upon the fearful pursued one are a snare's palm" (a hunter's noose).

The explanation of this has already passed in Surat Al ‘Imran. Then He, glory be to Him, described that Garden with another attribute, so He said: ﴿It has been prepared for those who believe in Allah and His messengers﴾. It is permissible that this sentence is a new (independent) sentence.

In this is evidence that entitlement to Paradise comes merely through faith in Allah and His messengers; but this is restricted by the proofs indicating that one does not deserve it except one who acts upon what Allah has obligated upon him and avoids what Allah has forbidden him, and these are many proofs in the Book and the Sunnah. The reference in His saying "That" is to what He, glory be to Him, has promised of forgiveness and Paradise, and it is a subject whose predicate is (p-1461) ﴿the bounty of Allah, which He gives to whom He wills﴾, that is, He gives it to whom He wills, giving it to him as a favour and kindness; and Allah is the Lord of mighty bounty, so He bestows favour upon whom He wills in what He wills. There is no preventer of what He gives, and no giver of what He withholds, and all good is in His hand, and He is the absolutely Generous and the Bountiful who does not withhold.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, made clear that what afflicts the servants of calamities has already been preceded by His decree and destiny, and is established in the Mother of the Book. So He said: ﴿No affliction befalls upon the earth﴾, from scarcity of rain, weakness of vegetation, and decrease of fruits.

Muqatil said: "Drought and scarcity of plants and fruits." It was also said: calamities in the crops. ﴿Nor in yourselves﴾. Qatadah said: "By ailments and sicknesses."

Muqatil also said: "The enforcement of prescribed punishments (hudud)."

Ibn Jurayj said: "Narrowness of livelihood." ﴿Except that it is in a Book﴾: in a place of nasb as a circumstantial (hal) from "affliction": that is, except in the state of being written in a Book, which is the Preserved Tablet. The clause ﴿before We bring it into being﴾ is in a place of jarr as an attribute of "Book." The pronoun in "nabra'ah" (We bring it into being) refers to the affliction, or to the souls, or to the earth, or to all of that. The meaning of "nabra'aha" is "We create it." ﴿Indeed that is easy for Allah﴾: that is, its recording in the Book, despite its multitude, is easy for Allah, not difficult.

﴿So that you do not despair over what has escaped you﴾: that is, We test you with that so that you do not grieve over what has escaped you of the world, nor exult in what He has given you of it, that is, granted you from it; for that passes away soon. Whatever passes away soon does not deserve to be rejoiced in its attainment nor grieved over its loss. And although everything is by the decree and destiny of Allah, "none can escape what has been written for him," and whatever is bound to occur inevitably, one does not deserve to rejoice in its attainment nor to grieve over its loss. It was also said that the grief and joy forbidden are those in which one transgresses into what is not permitted; otherwise there is no one who does not grieve and rejoice.

The majority read "bima atakum" with the long vowel (madd), that is, "gave you." Abu al-‘Aliyah, Nasr ibn ‘Asim, and Abu ‘Amr read it with qasr, that is, "came to you." Abu Hatim preferred the first reading, and Abu ‘Ubayd preferred the second. ﴿And Allah does not love any arrogant boaster﴾: that is, He does not love one who is characterised by these two attributes, which are arrogance (al-ikhtiyal) and boasting (al-iftikhar). It was said this is a censure of the joy in which its possessor becomes arrogant and exults; and it was said that whoever rejoices in worldly portions and they become great in his soul, he becomes arrogant and boastful with them. It was said: the arrogant one is he who looks at himself, and the boaster is he who looks at people with the eye of contempt.

The better course is to interpret these two attributes by their legal meaning and then their linguistic meaning; whoever has both of them in him is one whom Allah does not love.

﴿Those who are miserly and enjoin miserliness upon people﴾: the relative pronoun is in a place of raf‘ as the subject (mubtada'), and it is a new independent sentence with no connection to what precedes it, and the predicate is implied: that is, "those who are miserly, then Allah is free of need of them." This is indicated by His saying: ﴿And whoever turns away, then indeed Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾. It was also said that the relative clause is in a place of jarr as a substitute for "arrogant," but this is far-fetched, for this miserliness with what is in the hand and enjoining miserliness upon people is not the meaning of "arrogant boaster," neither linguistically nor legally. It was also said it is in a place of jarr as an attribute of it, and this too is far-fetched.

Sa‘id ibn Jubayr said: "Those who are miserly with knowledge and enjoin people to be miserly with it, so that they do not teach people anything." Zayd ibn Aslam said: "It is miserliness in paying the right of Allah." It was also said: it is miserliness in giving charity. Tawus said: "It is miserliness with what is in one's hands." It was also said that it intended the leaders of the Jews who were miserly in explaining the description of Muhammad ﷺ in their books, lest people believe in him and their food be lost; this was said by al-Suddi and al-Kalbi. The majority read "bil-bukhl" with a damma on the ba' and sukun on the kha'. Anas, ‘Ubayd ibn ‘Umayr, Yahya ibn Ya‘mar, Mujahid, Humayd, Ibn Muhaysin, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read it with two fathas, and this is the dialect of the Ansar. Abu al-‘Aliyah and Ibn al-Sumayfa‘ read it with a fatha on the ba' and sukun on the kha'. Nasr ibn ‘Asim read it with a damma on both, and all of these are dialects. ﴿And whoever turns away, then indeed Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾: that is, whoever turns away from spending, then Allah is free of need of him, praised by His creation, and that does not harm Him.

The majority read ﴿huwa al-ghaniyy﴾ with the pronoun of separation (dami̇r al-fasl) affirmed. Nafi‘ and Ibn ‘Amir read ﴿fa-inna Allaha al-ghaniyy﴾ with the pronoun omitted.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ‘Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿No affliction befalls upon the earth or in yourselves﴾, he said: "in religion and worldly life" ﴿except that it is in a Book before We bring it into being﴾, he said: "bring it into being" means "create it." ﴿So that you do not despair over what has escaped you﴾ of the world ﴿nor exult in what He has given you﴾ of it.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him regarding the verse, he said: "It is a matter that has been finished with before the souls are brought into being."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ‘Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu‘ab transmitted from him also regarding His saying: ﴿So that you do not despair over what has escaped you﴾ to the end of the verse, he said: "No one is free of grief and joy, but whoever is struck by an affliction makes it patience, and whoever receives good makes it gratitude."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him regarding the verse, he said: "It refers to the afflictions of livelihood, not the afflictions of religion; for He said: ﴿So that you do not despair over what has escaped you, nor exult in what He has given you﴾, and this is not among the afflictions of religion; He commanded them to grieve over the evil deed and rejoice in the good deed."
