There is no basis for restricting what is in the verse to such a thing; rather it is among what it applies to, either comprehensively or by way of substitution. ﴿And a Garden whose width is like the width of the heaven and earth﴾, that is, like their width. And if this is its measure in width, then what do you suppose of its length?

Al-Hasan said: "It means all the heavens and earths spread out, each one reaching to its companion." It was also said that the Garden whose width is this width is the garden of each one of the people of Paradise.

Ibn Kaysan said: "By it is meant one single garden of the gardens, and width is less than length. It is a habit of the Arabs to express a thing by its width without its length." Among this is the saying of the poet:

"As if the lands of Allah, though wide, upon the fearful pursued one are a snare's palm" (a hunter's noose).

The explanation of this has already passed in Surat Al ‘Imran. Then He, glory be to Him, described that Garden with another attribute, so He said: ﴿It has been prepared for those who believe in Allah and His messengers﴾. It is permissible that this sentence is a new (independent) sentence.

In this is evidence that entitlement to Paradise comes merely through faith in Allah and His messengers; but this is restricted by the proofs indicating that one does not deserve it except one who acts upon what Allah has obligated upon him and avoids what Allah has forbidden him, and these are many proofs in the Book and the Sunnah. The reference in His saying "That" is to what He, glory be to Him, has promised of forgiveness and Paradise, and it is a subject whose predicate is (p-1461) ﴿the bounty of Allah, which He gives to whom He wills﴾, that is, He gives it to whom He wills, giving it to him as a favour and kindness; and Allah is the Lord of mighty bounty, so He bestows favour upon whom He wills in what He wills. There is no preventer of what He gives, and no giver of what He withholds, and all good is in His hand, and He is the absolutely Generous and the Bountiful who does not withhold.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, made clear that what afflicts the servants of calamities has already been preceded by His decree and destiny, and is established in the Mother of the Book. So He said: ﴿No affliction befalls upon the earth﴾, from scarcity of rain, weakness of vegetation, and decrease of fruits.

Muqatil said: "Drought and scarcity of plants and fruits." It was also said: calamities in the crops. ﴿Nor in yourselves﴾. Qatadah said: "By ailments and sicknesses."

Muqatil also said: "The enforcement of prescribed punishments (hudud)."

Ibn Jurayj said: "Narrowness of livelihood." ﴿Except that it is in a Book﴾: in a place of nasb as a circumstantial (hal) from "affliction": that is, except in the state of being written in a Book, which is the Preserved Tablet. The clause ﴿before We bring it into being﴾ is in a place of jarr as an attribute of "Book." The pronoun in "nabra'ah" (We bring it into being) refers to the affliction, or to the souls, or to the earth, or to all of that. The meaning of "nabra'aha" is "We create it." ﴿Indeed that is easy for Allah﴾: that is, its recording in the Book, despite its multitude, is easy for Allah, not difficult.

﴿So that you do not despair over what has escaped you﴾: that is, We test you with that so that you do not grieve over what has escaped you of the world, nor exult in what He has given you of it, that is, granted you from it; for that passes away soon. Whatever passes away soon does not deserve to be rejoiced in its attainment nor grieved over its loss. And although everything is by the decree and destiny of Allah, "none can escape what has been written for him," and whatever is bound to occur inevitably, one does not deserve to rejoice in its attainment nor to grieve over its loss. It was also said that the grief and joy forbidden are those in which one transgresses into what is not permitted; otherwise there is no one who does not grieve and rejoice.

The majority read "bima atakum" with the long vowel (madd), that is, "gave you." Abu al-‘Aliyah, Nasr ibn ‘Asim, and Abu ‘Amr read it with qasr, that is, "came to you." Abu Hatim preferred the first reading, and Abu ‘Ubayd preferred the second. ﴿And Allah does not love any arrogant boaster﴾: that is, He does not love one who is characterised by these two attributes, which are arrogance (al-ikhtiyal) and boasting (al-iftikhar). It was said this is a censure of the joy in which its possessor becomes arrogant and exults; and it was said that whoever rejoices in worldly portions and they become great in his soul, he becomes arrogant and boastful with them. It was said: the arrogant one is he who looks at himself, and the boaster is he who looks at people with the eye of contempt.

The better course is to interpret these two attributes by their legal meaning and then their linguistic meaning; whoever has both of them in him is one whom Allah does not love.

﴿Those who are miserly and enjoin miserliness upon people﴾: the relative pronoun is in a place of raf‘ as the subject (mubtada'), and it is a new independent sentence with no connection to what precedes it, and the predicate is implied: that is, "those who are miserly, then Allah is free of need of them." This is indicated by His saying: ﴿And whoever turns away, then indeed Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾. It was also said that the relative clause is in a place of jarr as a substitute for "arrogant," but this is far-fetched, for this miserliness with what is in the hand and enjoining miserliness upon people is not the meaning of "arrogant boaster," neither linguistically nor legally. It was also said it is in a place of jarr as an attribute of it, and this too is far-fetched.

Sa‘id ibn Jubayr said: "Those who are miserly with knowledge and enjoin people to be miserly with it, so that they do not teach people anything." Zayd ibn Aslam said: "It is miserliness in paying the right of Allah." It was also said: it is miserliness in giving charity. Tawus said: "It is miserliness with what is in one's hands." It was also said that it intended the leaders of the Jews who were miserly in explaining the description of Muhammad ﷺ in their books, lest people believe in him and their food be lost; this was said by al-Suddi and al-Kalbi. The majority read "bil-bukhl" with a damma on the ba' and sukun on the kha'. Anas, ‘Ubayd ibn ‘Umayr, Yahya ibn Ya‘mar, Mujahid, Humayd, Ibn Muhaysin, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read it with two fathas, and this is the dialect of the Ansar. Abu al-‘Aliyah and Ibn al-Sumayfa‘ read it with a fatha on the ba' and sukun on the kha'. Nasr ibn ‘Asim read it with a damma on both, and all of these are dialects. ﴿And whoever turns away, then indeed Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾: that is, whoever turns away from spending, then Allah is free of need of him, praised by His creation, and that does not harm Him.

The majority read ﴿huwa al-ghaniyy﴾ with the pronoun of separation (dami̇r al-fasl) affirmed. Nafi‘ and Ibn ‘Amir read ﴿fa-inna Allaha al-ghaniyy﴾ with the pronoun omitted.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ‘Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿No affliction befalls upon the earth or in yourselves﴾, he said: "in religion and worldly life" ﴿except that it is in a Book before We bring it into being﴾, he said: "bring it into being" means "create it." ﴿So that you do not despair over what has escaped you﴾ of the world ﴿nor exult in what He has given you﴾ of it.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him regarding the verse, he said: "It is a matter that has been finished with before the souls are brought into being."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ‘Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu‘ab transmitted from him also regarding His saying: ﴿So that you do not despair over what has escaped you﴾ to the end of the verse, he said: "No one is free of grief and joy, but whoever is struck by an affliction makes it patience, and whoever receives good makes it gratitude."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him regarding the verse, he said: "It refers to the afflictions of livelihood, not the afflictions of religion; for He said: ﴿So that you do not despair over what has escaped you, nor exult in what He has given you﴾, and this is not among the afflictions of religion; He commanded them to grieve over the evil deed and rejoice in the good deed."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 57, verses 20–24:

His saying, ﴿Know that the life of this world is but play and amusement﴾. When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the state of the second group, and what occurred from them of disbelief and denial, this being because of their inclination towards the world and its influence, He made clear its worthlessness and that it is too base to be preferred over the Last Abode. Al-la‘ib (play) is falsehood, and al-lahw (amusement) is everything one diverts oneself with and then it goes away.

Qatadah said: "Play and amusement: eating and drinking."

Mujahid said: "Every play is amusement." It was also said: al-la‘ib is that which inclines one to the world, and al-lahw is that which distracts one from the Hereafter and occupies one away from it. It was also said: al-la‘ib is acquisition (iqtina’), and al-lahw is women. The verification of this has already been discussed in Surat al-An‘am. Al-zinah (adornment) is adorning oneself with the goods of this world without action for the Hereafter. ﴿And boasting among you﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read tafakhur with tanwin, and the adverbial phrase is an attribute of it, or an object of it. Al-Sulami read it with idafah: that is, one of you boasts of it over another. It was said: they boast of physical form and strength, and it was said: of lineages and noble descent, as the Arabs used to do. ﴿And competition in wealth and children﴾, that is, they vie with one another in their wealth and children and exalt themselves through that over the poor.

Then, glory be to Him, made for this account a likeness and coined for it an example, so He said: ﴿like the example of rain whose vegetation pleases the disbelievers﴾, that is, like the example of rain whose vegetation pleases the farmers. What is meant by "the disbelievers" here is the farmers, because they cover (yakfuruna) the seed, that is, they cover it with soil. The meaning of "its vegetation" is the plant produced by it. ﴿Then it dries up﴾, that is, it withers after its greenness and dries out. ﴿So you see it turning yellow﴾, that is, changed from what it was of greenness; the brightness has turned to a yellow colour and wilting. ﴿Then it becomes debris﴾, that is, crumbled fragments, broken and shattered after its drying. The interpretation of this parable has already been given in Surat Yunus and al-Kahf. The meaning is that the life of this world is like a crop which pleases those who look at it because of its greenness and abundant freshness.

Then it is not long before it becomes stubble, chaff, as though it had never been.

It is also read as musfarran, and the kaf is in a place of nasb as a circumstantial (hal), or in a place of raf‘ as being a predicate after a predicate, or the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada').

Then, when He, glory be to Him, mentioned the worthlessness of the world and the swiftness of its passing, He mentioned what He has prepared for the disobedient in the Hereafter, so He said: ﴿And in the Hereafter there is severe punishment﴾, and He followed it with what He has prepared for the people of obedience, so He said: ﴿and forgiveness from Allah and approval﴾. The indefiniteness in both is for magnification.

Qatadah said: "Severe punishment is for the enemies of Allah. And forgiveness from Allah and approval is for His friends and the people of His obedience."

Al-Farra' said: The estimation in the verse is either "severe punishment" or "forgiveness," so one does not stop at "severe."

Then, after intimidation and encouragement, He, glory be to Him, mentioned the worthlessness of the world, so He said: ﴿And the life of this world is nothing but the goods of delusion﴾ for one who is deceived by it and does not work for his Hereafter.

Sa‘id ibn Jubayr said: "The goods of delusion are for one who does not occupy himself with seeking the Hereafter; and whoever occupies himself with seeking it, for him is the provision (mata‘ balagh) to what is better than it."

This sentence confirms and emphasises the preceding parable.

[p. 1462] Allah's saying, ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs﴾, meaning with manifest miracles and clear laws. ﴿And We sent down with them the Book﴾: here "the Book" is used generically (jins, a category), so it includes the scripture of every messenger. ﴿And the Balance﴾ "so that people may uphold justice." Qatadah and Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: the Balance is justice. The meaning is that He commanded them to act justly, as in His saying ﴿And the heaven He raised high, and He set up the Balance﴾ [al-Rahman: 7], and His saying ﴿Allah is He who sent down the Book with truth and the Balance﴾ [al-Shura: 17]. Ibn Zayd said: it is that by which things are weighed and through which dealings are conducted. The meaning of ﴿so that people may uphold justice﴾ is that they follow what they were commanded regarding justice, so that they deal with one another fairly. Al-qist means justice, and this indicates that the intended meaning of "the Balance" is justice. The meaning of "sending it down" is sending down its causes and requirements.

On the view that the Balance refers to the instrument used for weighing, then "sending it down" means guiding people to it and inspiring them to weigh with it. In that case the expression is of the type of the line of poetry:

*"I fed her straw and cold water"*

﴿And We sent down iron﴾, meaning We created it, as in His saying ﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ [al-Zumar: 6]. The meaning is that He created it from ores and taught people how to craft it. It was said that it was sent down together with Adam. It contains great might, because weapons of war are made from it. Al-Zajjaj said: by it one defends oneself and wages war. The meaning is that instruments of defence and instruments of striking are made from it. Mujahid said: in it there is protection and weaponry. ﴿And benefits for people﴾ means that they benefit from it in many of their needs, such as knives, axes, needles, and the tools of farming, carpentry and building.

﴿And that Allah may know who supports Him and His messengers unseen﴾ is coordinated with His saying "so that people may uphold justice". That is: We sent Our messengers, and We did such-and-such, so that people may uphold justice and so that Allah may know. It was also said that it is coordinated with a presumed cause, as if it were said: "so that they may learn it, and so that Allah may know." The first view is preferable.

The meaning is that Allah commanded, in the Book He sent down, that His religion and His messengers be supported. Whoever supports His religion and His messengers, He knows him as a supporter, and whoever disobeys, He knows him to be otherwise. ﴿Unseen﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (hal), either of the subject of "supports" or of its object: that is, absent from them, or they absent from Him. ﴿Indeed Allah is Strong, Mighty﴾, meaning able over everything and overpowering everything. He has no need that any of His servants support Him or support His messengers. Rather, He imposed this upon them so that they benefit from it if they comply, and so that they obtain what He has promised His obedient servants.

﴿And We certainly sent Noah and Abraham﴾. When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the sending of messengers in general terms, He here alluded to a kind of detail: He mentioned His sending of messengers to Noah and Abraham, and He repeated the oath for emphasis. ﴿And We placed in their descendants prophethood and the Book﴾, meaning We placed among them prophethood and the scriptures sent down to the prophets from among them. It was said that He made some of them prophets and some of them reciters of the Book. ﴿So among them is one who is guided﴾, meaning among the descendants is one who followed the guidance of Noah and Abraham. It was said the meaning is: among those to whom the prophets were sent, from the peoples of the prophets, is one who is guided by what the prophets brought of guidance. ﴿And many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾, meaning they have departed from obedience.

﴿Then We followed up after them with Our messengers﴾, meaning We sent, following after the descendants or after Noah and Abraham, Our messengers whom We sent to the nations, such as Moses, Elias, David, Solomon and others. ﴿And We followed up with Jesus, son of Mary﴾, meaning We sent one messenger after another until it reached Jesus, son of Mary, who was from the descendants of Abraham through his mother. ﴿And We gave him the Gospel﴾: this is the Book that Allah sent down to him. Its derivation has already been mentioned in Surat Al 'Imran.

The majority read al-Injil with a kasra on the hamzah, and al-Hasan read it with a fatha on the hamzah. ﴿And We placed in the hearts of those who followed him compassion and mercy﴾. Those who followed him were the disciples (al-hawariyyun). Allah placed in their hearts affection for one another, and mercy by which they showed mercy to each other, unlike the Jews, who were not like that. The root of ra'fah is gentleness, and rahmah is tenderness. It was said that ra'fah is a more intense form of mercy. ﴿But monasticism, they innovated it﴾. The accusative of "monasticism" (rahbaniyyatan) is on the basis of the verb being implied (ishtighal): that is, "and they innovated a monasticism which they innovated." It is not coordinated with what precedes it. It was said that it is coordinated with what precedes it, meaning: "and We placed in their hearts compassion, mercy and monasticism, an innovation from their own selves."

The first view is preferable, and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi and others preferred it. The clause ﴿We did not prescribe it for them﴾ is a second attribute of "monasticism", or a resumptive clause affirming that it was an innovation from their own side. The meaning is: We did not impose it upon them. Rahbaniyyah may be read with a fatha or a damma on the letter ra', and both readings are attested. With a fatha, it means fear, from ar-rahb (dread). With a damma, it is related to ar-ruhban (monks). This is because they exaggerated in worship and imposed hardships on themselves, abstaining from food, drink and marriage, and they clung to caves and monasteries. This was because their kings had altered and changed things, and a small group remained who withdrew into solitude and devotion. This meaning was mentioned by al-Dahhak, Qatadah and others.

﴿Except seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾. The exception here is disconnected (munqati', an exception not from the same category). That is: We did not prescribe it for them ourselves at all, but they innovated it seeking the pleasure of Allah.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of ﴿We did not prescribe it for them﴾ is that We did not prescribe anything for them whatsoever. He said: "except seeking the pleasure of Allah" may be a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in "We prescribed it", and the meaning is: "We did not prescribe for them except seeking the pleasure of Allah." ﴿But they did not observe it with its proper observance﴾, meaning they did not observe this monasticism which they innovated from their own side. Rather, they neglected it and disbelieved in the religion of Jesus, and entered the religion of the kings who had altered and changed things and abandoned asceticism. Only a few of them remained upon the religion of Jesus, and they are the ones intended by His saying ﴿So We gave those of them who believed their reward﴾, which they deserve through faith. That is because they believed in Jesus and remained steadfast in his religion until they believed in Muhammad (ﷺ) when Allah sent him. ﴿And many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾, meaning they departed from faith in what they were commanded to believe in. The blame directed at them, on the assumption that the exception is disconnected, is that they had obligated themselves to monasticism, believing it to be obedience and that Allah was pleased with it. So abandoning it and not observing it with its proper observance indicates their indifference to what they believed to be their religion.

As for the view that the exception is connected (muttasil), and the sense is: "We did not prescribe it for them for any reason except that they might seek the pleasure of Allah, after We had enabled them to innovate it," then the blame is obvious.

Then, glory be to Him, He commanded the believers, addressing those who had come after the earlier messengers, to have taqwa and to believe in Muhammad (ﷺ). He said: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah﴾, by abstaining from what He has forbidden you, ﴿and believe in His Messenger﴾ Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿He will give you a double portion of His mercy﴾, meaning two shares of His mercy because of your belief in His Messenger after your belief in the messengers before him. The root of kifl is portion and share. Its interpretation has already been discussed in Surat an-Nisa'. ﴿And He will make for you a light by which you will walk﴾, meaning on the Path, as He said ﴿Their light runs before them﴾. It was also said the meaning is: He will make for you a clear way in the religion by which you will be guided. ﴿And He will forgive you﴾ your past sins. ﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning abundantly forgiving and merciful.

﴿So that the People of the Book may know﴾. The lam (of purpose) is connected to what preceded, the command to believe and to have taqwa. The sense is: "Fear Allah and believe, He will give you such-and-such, so that those among the People of the Book who did not fear Allah and did not believe may know that they have no power over any of the bounty of Allah." The "la" in "li-'allā" is an emphatic extra particle (za'idah li-l-ta'kid), as stated by al-Farra', al-Akhfash and others. The meaning is: so that the People of the Book may know that they are not able to attain any of the bounty of Allah that He has bestowed upon whoever believes in Muhammad (ﷺ), and they are not able to repel that bounty which Allah has bestowed upon those who deserve it. Abd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim, al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman transmitted, through the chains of Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: 'O 'Abd Allah!' He said: 'The best of people is the one whose deeds are best when they comprehend their religion. O 'Abd Allah, do you know which of the people is most knowledgeable?' I said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'The most knowledgeable of people is the one who sees the truth most clearly when people differ, even if he falls short in deeds, even if he crawls on his backside. Those before us differed into seventy-two sects, of which three were saved and the rest perished: a sect which supported the kings and fought them in the cause of the religion of Allah and of Jesus, son of Mary; a sect which had no ability to support the kings, so they stayed among their people, calling them to the religion of Allah and the religion of Jesus, and the kings killed them and sawed them apart with saws; and a sect which had no ability to support the kings nor to remain among them, so they wandered in the mountains and lived there as monks. These are the ones of whom Allah said: ﴿But monasticism, they innovated it; We did not prescribe it for them, except seeking the pleasure of Allah. Al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim, al-Tirmidhi in *Nawadir al-Usul*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: After 'Isa (Jesus), there were kings who altered the Torah and the Gospel. Among them were believers who read the Torah and the Gospel. It was said to their kings, "We find nothing more severe than the abuse that these people heap upon us. So summon them, and let them recite as we recite and believe as we believe." So the kings summoned them, gathered them, and offered them the choice of being killed or of abandoning the recitation of the Torah and the Gospel, except for what they had altered from them. They said, "What do you want from us with this? Leave us alone." A group among them said, "Build us a pillar, then raise us up to it, and give us something with which to lift up our food and drink, and we will not return to you." Another group said, "Leave us to travel through the earth and wander, and to eat what the wild beasts eat and drink what they drink. If you have power over us in your land, then kill us." Another group said, "Build us houses in the wilderness, and let us dig wells and cultivate herbs. Then we will not return to you nor pass by you." There was no tribe that did not have a close relative among them, and so they did this. Then Allah revealed: ﴿Monasticism, which they invented; We did not prescribe it for them, but they sought the pleasure of Allah, and they did not observe it with its proper observance﴾. Others, from among those who worshipped in polytheism, and when those who had passed away had died, said, "We will worship as so-and-so worshipped, and wander as so-and-so wandered, and take houses as so-and-so took houses," while they remained upon their polytheism and had no knowledge of the faith of those whom they followed. When the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent and only a few of them remained, the monk of the cell came down from his cell, the wanderer came back from his wandering, and the monk of the monastery came down from his monastery. They believed in him and affirmed him. Then Allah said: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah and believe in His Messenger; He will give you a double portion of His mercy﴾, meaning two rewards for their belief in 'Isa, their striving of themselves, and the Torah and the Gospel, and for their belief in Muhammad and their affirmation of him. ﴿And make for you a light by which you will walk﴾, meaning the Qur'an, and their following of the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ahmad, al-Hakim, al-Tirmidhi, Abu Ya'la, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* narrated from Anas that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Every nation has a monasticism, and the monasticism of this nation is jihad in the way of Allah."

*"I fed her straw and cold water"*

Its derivation has already been mentioned in Surat Al 'Imran.

The majority read al-Injil with a kasra on the hamzah, and al-Hasan read it with a fatha on the hamzah. ﴿And We placed in the hearts of those who followed him compassion and mercy﴾. The accusative of "monasticism" (rahbaniyyatan) is on the basis of the verb being implied (ishtighal): that is, "and they innovated a monasticism which they innovated." This is because they exaggerated in worship and imposed hardships on themselves, abstaining from food, drink and marriage, and they clung to caves and monasteries. This was because their kings had altered and changed things, and a small group remained who withdrew into solitude and devotion. This meaning was mentioned by al-Dahhak, Qatadah and others.

﴿Except seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾. The exception here is disconnected (munqati', an exception not from the same category). That is: We did not prescribe it for them ourselves at all, but they innovated it seeking the pleasure of Allah.

He said: "except seeking the pleasure of Allah" may be a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in "We prescribed it", and the meaning is: "We did not prescribe for them except seeking the pleasure of Allah." ﴿But they did not observe it with its proper observance﴾, meaning they did not observe this monasticism which they innovated from their own side. Only a few of them remained upon the religion of Jesus, and they are the ones intended by His saying ﴿So We gave those of them who believed their reward﴾, which they deserve through faith. That is because they believed in Jesus and remained steadfast in his religion until they believed in Muhammad (ﷺ) when Allah sent him. ﴿And many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾, meaning they departed from faith in what they were commanded to believe in. The blame directed at them, on the assumption that the exception is disconnected, is that they had obligated themselves to monasticism, believing it to be obedience and that Allah was pleased with it. It was said the meaning is: among those to whom the prophets were sent, from the peoples of the prophets, is one who is guided by what the prophets brought of guidance. ﴿And many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾, meaning they have departed from obedience.

﴿Then We followed up after them with Our messengers﴾, meaning We sent, following after the descendants or after Noah and Abraham, Our messengers whom We sent to the nations, such as Moses, Elias, David, Solomon and others. ﴿And We followed up with Jesus, son of Mary﴾, meaning We sent one messenger after another until it reached Jesus, son of Mary, who was from the descendants of Abraham through his mother. ﴿And We gave him the Gospel﴾: this is the Book that Allah sent down to him. Its derivation has already been mentioned in Surat Al 'Imran.

The majority read al-Injil with a kasra on the hamzah, and al-Hasan read it with a fatha on the hamzah. ﴿And We placed in the hearts of those who followed him compassion and mercy﴾. Those who followed him were the disciples (al-hawariyyun). Allah placed in their hearts affection for one another, and mercy by which they showed mercy to each other, unlike the Jews, who were not like that. The root of ra'fah is gentleness, and rahmah is tenderness. It was said that ra'fah is a more intense form of mercy. ﴿But monasticism, they innovated it﴾. The accusative of "monasticism" (rahbaniyyatan) is on the basis of the verb being implied (ishtighal): that is, "and they innovated a monasticism which they innovated." It is not coordinated with what precedes it. It was said that it is coordinated with what precedes it, meaning: "and We placed in their hearts compassion, mercy and monasticism, an innovation from their own selves."

The first view is preferable, and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi and others preferred it. The clause ﴿We did not prescribe it for them﴾ is a second attribute of "monasticism", or a resumptive clause affirming that it was an innovation from their own side. The meaning is: We did not impose it upon them. Rahbaniyyah may be read with a fatha or a damma on the letter ra', and both readings are attested. With a fatha, it means fear, from ar-rahb (dread). With a damma, it is related to ar-ruhban (monks). This is because they exaggerated in worship and imposed hardships on themselves, abstaining from food, drink and marriage, and they clung to caves and monasteries. This was because their kings had altered and changed things, and a small group remained who withdrew into solitude and devotion. This meaning was mentioned by al-Dahhak, Qatadah and others.

﴿Except seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾. The exception here is disconnected (munqati', an exception not from the same category). That is: We did not prescribe it for them ourselves at all, but they innovated it seeking the pleasure of Allah.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of ﴿We did not prescribe it for them﴾ is that We did not prescribe anything for them whatsoever. He said: "except seeking the pleasure of Allah" may be a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in "We prescribed it", and the meaning is: "We did not prescribe for them except seeking the pleasure of Allah." ﴿But they did not observe it with its proper observance﴾, meaning they did not observe this monasticism which they innovated from their own side. Rather, they neglected it and disbelieved in the religion of Jesus, and entered the religion of the kings who had altered and changed things and abandoned asceticism. Only a few of them remained upon the religion of Jesus, and they are the ones intended by His saying ﴿So We gave those of them who believed their reward﴾, which they deserve through faith. That is because they believed in Jesus and remained steadfast in his religion until they believed in Muhammad (ﷺ) when Allah sent him. ﴿And many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾, meaning they departed from faith in what they were commanded to believe in. The blame directed at them, on the assumption that the exception is disconnected, is that they had obligated themselves to monasticism, believing it to be obedience and that Allah was pleased with it. So abandoning it and not observing it with its proper observance indicates their indifference to what they believed to be their religion.

As for the view that the exception is connected (muttasil), and the sense is: "We did not prescribe it for them for any reason except that they might seek the pleasure of Allah, after We had enabled them to innovate it," then the blame is obvious.

Then, glory be to Him, He commanded the believers, addressing those who had come after the earlier messengers, to have taqwa and to believe in Muhammad (ﷺ). He said: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah﴾, by abstaining from what He has forbidden you, ﴿and believe in His Messenger﴾ Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿He will give you a double portion of His mercy﴾, meaning two shares of His mercy because of your belief in His Messenger after your belief in the messengers before him. The root of kifl is portion and share. Its interpretation has already been discussed in Surat an-Nisa'. ﴿And He will make for you a light by which you will walk﴾, meaning on the Path, as He said ﴿Their light runs before them﴾. It was also said the meaning is: He will make for you a clear way in the religion by which you will be guided. ﴿And He will forgive you﴾ your past sins. ﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning abundantly forgiving and merciful.

﴿So that the People of the Book may know﴾. The lam (of purpose) is connected to what preceded, the command to believe and to have taqwa. The sense is: "Fear Allah and believe, He will give you such-and-such, so that those among the People of the Book who did not fear Allah and did not believe may know that they have no power over any of the bounty of Allah." The "la" in "li-'allā" is an emphatic extra particle (za'idah li-l-ta'kid), as stated by al-Farra', al-Akhfash and others. The "an" in "an la yaqdiruna" is the light form of the heavy an (mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah), whose noun is an omitted pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), and its predicate is what follows it. The clause is in the accusative position as the object of "may know". The meaning is: so that the People of the Book may know that they are not able to attain any of the bounty of Allah that He has bestowed upon whoever believes in Muhammad (ﷺ), and they are not able to repel that bounty which Allah has bestowed upon those who deserve it. The clause ﴿and that bounty is in the hand of Allah﴾ is coordinated with the preceding clause: that is, so that they may know that they are not able, and so that they may know that bounty is in the hand of Allah, glory be to Him. His saying ﴿He gives it to whom He wills﴾ is a second predicate of "an", or it is the predicate, and the prepositional phrase is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state. ﴿And Allah is the Owner of great bounty﴾: this clause affirms the content of what precedes it. Bounty here means the double reward He bestowed upon those who had taqwa and believed in His Messenger.

Al-Kalbi said: it is the provision of Allah. It was said: the blessings of Allah which cannot be counted. It was said: it is Islam. It has been said that the "la" in "li-'allā" is not extra, and that the pronoun in "la yaqdiruna" refers to the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions. The meaning is: so that the People of the Book do not believe that the Prophet and the believers have no power over any of the bounty of Allah, which is an expression for what they were given. The first view is preferable.

Ibn Mas'ud read "li-kay la ya'lama" (so that he may not know). Khattab ibn 'Abd Allah read "li-an ya'lama" (that he may know). 'Ikrimah read "li-ya'lama" (that he may know). It was also read "li-yalla" with the hamzah changed to a ya', and it was read with a fatha on the lam.

Abd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim, al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman transmitted, through the chains of Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: 'O 'Abd Allah!' I said: 'At your service, O Messenger of Allah,' three times. He said: 'Do you know which of the firmest handholds of Islam is the strongest?' I said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'The best of people is the one whose deeds are best when they comprehend their religion. O 'Abd Allah, do you know which of the people is most knowledgeable?' I said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'The most knowledgeable of people is the one who sees the truth most clearly when people differ, even if he falls short in deeds, even if he crawls on his backside. Those before us differed into seventy-two sects, of which three were saved and the rest perished: a sect which supported the kings and fought them in the cause of the religion of Allah and of Jesus, son of Mary; a sect which had no ability to support the kings, so they stayed among their people, calling them to the religion of Allah and the religion of Jesus, and the kings killed them and sawed them apart with saws; and a sect which had no ability to support the kings nor to remain among them, so they wandered in the mountains and lived there as monks. These are the ones of whom Allah said: ﴿But monasticism, they innovated it; We did not prescribe it for them, except seeking the pleasure of Allah. But they did not observe it with its proper observance. So We gave those of them who believed their reward; and many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾. Those who believed in Me and affirmed Me are the ones who believed, and ﴿many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾ are those who denied Me and disbelieved in Me.'"

Al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim, al-Tirmidhi in *Nawadir al-Usul*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: After 'Isa (Jesus), there were kings who altered the Torah and the Gospel. Among them were believers who read the Torah and the Gospel. It was said to their kings, "We find nothing more severe than the abuse that these people heap upon us. They recite, ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾, ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the wrongdoers﴾, ﴿those are the defiantly disobedient﴾, along with the faults they find in our deeds in their recitation. So summon them, and let them recite as we recite and believe as we believe." So the kings summoned them, gathered them, and offered them the choice of being killed or of abandoning the recitation of the Torah and the Gospel, except for what they had altered from them. They said, "What do you want from us with this? Leave us alone." A group among them said, "Build us a pillar, then raise us up to it, and give us something with which to lift up our food and drink, and we will not return to you." Another group said, "Leave us to travel through the earth and wander, and to eat what the wild beasts eat and drink what they drink. If you have power over us in your land, then kill us." Another group said, "Build us houses in the wilderness, and let us dig wells and cultivate herbs. Then we will not return to you nor pass by you." There was no tribe that did not have a close relative among them, and so they did this. Then Allah revealed: ﴿Monasticism, which they invented; We did not prescribe it for them, but they sought the pleasure of Allah, and they did not observe it with its proper observance﴾. When the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent and only a few of them remained, the monk of the cell came down from his cell, the wanderer came back from his wandering, and the monk of the monastery came down from his monastery. They believed in him and affirmed him. Ahmad, al-Hakim, al-Tirmidhi, Abu Ya'la, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* narrated from Anas that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Every nation has a monasticism, and the monasticism of this nation is jihad in the way of Allah."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Umar regarding His saying ﴿He will give you a double portion of His mercy﴾ that he said: "The *kifl* is three hundred and fifty parts of the mercy of Allah."

Qatadah and Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: the Balance is justice. The meaning is that He commanded them to act justly, as in His saying ﴿And the heaven He raised high, and He set up the Balance﴾ [al-Rahman: 7], and His saying ﴿Allah is He who sent down the Book with truth and the Balance﴾ [al-Shura: 17]. Ibn Zayd said: it is that by which things are weighed and through which dealings are conducted. The meaning of ﴿so that people may uphold justice﴾ is that they follow what they were commanded regarding justice, so that they deal with one another fairly. Al-qist means justice, and this indicates that the intended meaning of "the Balance" is justice. The meaning of "sending it down" is sending down its causes and requirements.

On the view that the Balance refers to the instrument used for weighing, then "sending it down" means guiding people to it and inspiring them to weigh with it. In that case the expression is of the type of the line of poetry:

*"I fed her straw and cold water"*

﴿And We sent down iron﴾, meaning We created it, as in His saying ﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ [al-Zumar: 6]. The meaning is that He created it from ores and taught people how to craft it. It was said that it was sent down together with Adam. It contains great might, because weapons of war are made from it. Al-Zajjaj said: by it one defends oneself and wages war. The meaning is that instruments of defence and instruments of striking are made from it. Mujahid said: in it there is protection and weaponry. ﴿And benefits for people﴾ means that they benefit from it in many of their needs, such as knives, axes, needles, and the tools of farming, carpentry and building.

﴿And that Allah may know who supports Him and His messengers unseen﴾ is coordinated with His saying "so that people may uphold justice". That is: We sent Our messengers, and We did such-and-such, so that people may uphold justice and so that Allah may know. It was also said that it is coordinated with a presumed cause, as if it were said: "so that they may learn it, and so that Allah may know." The first view is preferable.

The meaning is that Allah commanded, in the Book He sent down, that His religion and His messengers be supported. He has no need that any of His servants support Him or support His messengers. Rather, He imposed this upon them so that they benefit from it if they comply, and so that they obtain what He has promised His obedient servants.

Then Allah said: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah and believe in His Messenger; He will give you a double portion of His mercy﴾, meaning two rewards for their belief in 'Isa, their striving of themselves, and the Torah and the Gospel, and for their belief in Muhammad and their affirmation of him. ﴿And make for you a light by which you will walk﴾, meaning the Qur'an, and their following of the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ahmad, al-Hakim, al-Tirmidhi, Abu Ya'la, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* narrated from Anas that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Every nation has a monasticism, and the monasticism of this nation is jihad in the way of Allah."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari regarding His saying ﴿kiflayn﴾ (two portions, كِفْلَيْنِ) that he said: "Two-fold." And it is in the language of Abyssinia (Ethiopia).

Al-Firyabi, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Umar regarding His saying ﴿He will give you a double portion of His mercy﴾ that he said: "The *kifl* is three hundred and fifty parts of the mercy of Allah."

[p. 1462] Allah's saying, ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs﴾, meaning with manifest miracles and clear laws. ﴿And We sent down with them the Book﴾: here "the Book" is used generically (jins, a category), so it includes the scripture of every messenger. ﴿And the Balance﴾ "so that people may uphold justice." Qatadah and Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: the Balance is justice. The meaning is that He commanded them to act justly, as in His saying ﴿And the heaven He raised high, and He set up the Balance﴾ [al-Rahman: 7], and His saying ﴿Allah is He who sent down the Book with truth and the Balance﴾ [al-Shura: 17]. Ibn Zayd said: it is that by which things are weighed and through which dealings are conducted. The meaning of ﴿so that people may uphold justice﴾ is that they follow what they were commanded regarding justice, so that they deal with one another fairly. Al-qist means justice, and this indicates that the intended meaning of "the Balance" is justice. The meaning of "sending it down" is sending down its causes and requirements.

On the view that the Balance refers to the instrument used for weighing, then "sending it down" means guiding people to it and inspiring them to weigh with it. In that case the expression is of the type of the line of poetry:

*"I fed her straw and cold water"*

﴿And We sent down iron﴾, meaning We created it, as in His saying ﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ [al-Zumar: 6]. The meaning is that He created it from ores and taught people how to craft it. It was said that it was sent down together with Adam. It contains great might, because weapons of war are made from it. Al-Zajjaj said: by it one defends oneself and wages war. The meaning is that instruments of defence and instruments of striking are made from it. Mujahid said: in it there is protection and weaponry. ﴿And benefits for people﴾ means that they benefit from it in many of their needs, such as knives, axes, needles, and the tools of farming, carpentry and building.

﴿And that Allah may know who supports Him and His messengers unseen﴾ is coordinated with His saying "so that people may uphold justice". That is: We sent Our messengers, and We did such-and-such, so that people may uphold justice and so that Allah may know. It was also said that it is coordinated with a presumed cause, as if it were said: "so that they may learn it, and so that Allah may know." The first view is preferable.

The meaning is that Allah commanded, in the Book He sent down, that His religion and His messengers be supported. Whoever supports His religion and His messengers, He knows him as a supporter, and whoever disobeys, He knows him to be otherwise. ﴿Unseen﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (hal), either of the subject of "supports" or of its object: that is, absent from them, or they absent from Him. ﴿Indeed Allah is Strong, Mighty﴾, meaning able over everything and overpowering everything. He has no need that any of His servants support Him or support His messengers. Rather, He imposed this upon them so that they benefit from it if they comply, and so that they obtain what He has promised His obedient servants.

﴿And We certainly sent Noah and Abraham﴾. When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the sending of messengers in general terms, He here alluded to a kind of detail: He mentioned His sending of messengers to Noah and Abraham, and He repeated the oath for emphasis. ﴿And We placed in their descendants prophethood and the Book﴾, meaning We placed among them prophethood and the scriptures sent down to the prophets from among them. It was said that He made some of them prophets and some of them reciters of the Book. ﴿So among them is one who is guided﴾, meaning among the descendants is one who followed the guidance of Noah and Abraham. It was said the meaning is: among those to whom the prophets were sent, from the peoples of the prophets, is one who is guided by what the prophets brought of guidance. ﴿And many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾, meaning they have departed from obedience.

﴿Then We followed up after them with Our messengers﴾, meaning We sent, following after the descendants or after Noah and Abraham, Our messengers whom We sent to the nations, such as Moses, Elias, David, Solomon and others. ﴿And We followed up with Jesus, son of Mary﴾, meaning We sent one messenger after another until it reached Jesus, son of Mary, who was from the descendants of Abraham through his mother. ﴿And We gave him the Gospel﴾: this is the Book that Allah sent down to him. Its derivation has already been mentioned in Surat Al 'Imran.

The majority read al-Injil with a kasra on the hamzah, and al-Hasan read it with a fatha on the hamzah. ﴿And We placed in the hearts of those who followed him compassion and mercy﴾. Those who followed him were the disciples (al-hawariyyun). Allah placed in their hearts affection for one another, and mercy by which they showed mercy to each other, unlike the Jews, who were not like that. The root of ra'fah is gentleness, and rahmah is tenderness. It was said that ra'fah is a more intense form of mercy. ﴿But monasticism, they innovated it﴾. The accusative of "monasticism" (rahbaniyyatan) is on the basis of the verb being implied (ishtighal): that is, "and they innovated a monasticism which they innovated." It is not coordinated with what precedes it. It was said that it is coordinated with what precedes it, meaning: "and We placed in their hearts compassion, mercy and monasticism, an innovation from their own selves."

The first view is preferable, and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi and others preferred it. The clause ﴿We did not prescribe it for them﴾ is a second attribute of "monasticism", or a resumptive clause affirming that it was an innovation from their own side. The meaning is: We did not impose it upon them. Rahbaniyyah may be read with a fatha or a damma on the letter ra', and both readings are attested. With a fatha, it means fear, from ar-rahb (dread). With a damma, it is related to ar-ruhban (monks). This is because they exaggerated in worship and imposed hardships on themselves, abstaining from food, drink and marriage, and they clung to caves and monasteries. This was because their kings had altered and changed things, and a small group remained who withdrew into solitude and devotion. This meaning was mentioned by al-Dahhak, Qatadah and others.

﴿Except seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾. The exception here is disconnected (munqati', an exception not from the same category). That is: We did not prescribe it for them ourselves at all, but they innovated it seeking the pleasure of Allah.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of ﴿We did not prescribe it for them﴾ is that We did not prescribe anything for them whatsoever. He said: "except seeking the pleasure of Allah" may be a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in "We prescribed it", and the meaning is: "We did not prescribe for them except seeking the pleasure of Allah." ﴿But they did not observe it with its proper observance﴾, meaning they did not observe this monasticism which they innovated from their own side. Rather, they neglected it and disbelieved in the religion of Jesus, and entered the religion of the kings who had altered and changed things and abandoned asceticism. Only a few of them remained upon the religion of Jesus, and they are the ones intended by His saying ﴿So We gave those of them who believed their reward﴾, which they deserve through faith. That is because they believed in Jesus and remained steadfast in his religion until they believed in Muhammad (ﷺ) when Allah sent him. ﴿And many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾, meaning they departed from faith in what they were commanded to believe in. The blame directed at them, on the assumption that the exception is disconnected, is that they had obligated themselves to monasticism, believing it to be obedience and that Allah was pleased with it. So abandoning it and not observing it with its proper observance indicates their indifference to what they believed to be their religion.

As for the view that the exception is connected (muttasil), and the sense is: "We did not prescribe it for them for any reason except that they might seek the pleasure of Allah, after We had enabled them to innovate it," then the blame is obvious.

Then, glory be to Him, He commanded the believers, addressing those who had come after the earlier messengers, to have taqwa and to believe in Muhammad (ﷺ). He said: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah﴾, by abstaining from what He has forbidden you, ﴿and believe in His Messenger﴾ Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿He will give you a double portion of His mercy﴾, meaning two shares of His mercy because of your belief in His Messenger after your belief in the messengers before him. The root of kifl is portion and share. Its interpretation has already been discussed in Surat an-Nisa'. ﴿And He will make for you a light by which you will walk﴾, meaning on the Path, as He said ﴿Their light runs before them﴾. It was also said the meaning is: He will make for you a clear way in the religion by which you will be guided. ﴿And He will forgive you﴾ your past sins. ﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning abundantly forgiving and merciful.

﴿So that the People of the Book may know﴾. The lam (of purpose) is connected to what preceded, the command to believe and to have taqwa. The sense is: "Fear Allah and believe, He will give you such-and-such, so that those among the People of the Book who did not fear Allah and did not believe may know that they have no power over any of the bounty of Allah." The "la" in "li-'allā" is an emphatic extra particle (za'idah li-l-ta'kid), as stated by al-Farra', al-Akhfash and others. The "an" in "an la yaqdiruna" is the light form of the heavy an (mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah), whose noun is an omitted pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), and its predicate is what follows it. The clause is in the accusative position as the object of "may know". The meaning is: so that the People of the Book may know that they are not able to attain any of the bounty of Allah that He has bestowed upon whoever believes in Muhammad (ﷺ), and they are not able to repel that bounty which Allah has bestowed upon those who deserve it. The clause ﴿and that bounty is in the hand of Allah﴾ is coordinated with the preceding clause: that is, so that they may know that they are not able, and so that they may know that bounty is in the hand of Allah, glory be to Him. His saying ﴿He gives it to whom He wills﴾ is a second predicate of "an", or it is the predicate, and the prepositional phrase is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state. ﴿And Allah is the Owner of great bounty﴾: this clause affirms the content of what precedes it. Bounty here means the double reward He bestowed upon those who had taqwa and believed in His Messenger.

Al-Kalbi said: it is the provision of Allah. It was said: the blessings of Allah which cannot be counted. It was said: it is Islam. It has been said that the "la" in "li-'allā" is not extra, and that the pronoun in "la yaqdiruna" refers to the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions. The meaning is: so that the People of the Book do not believe that the Prophet and the believers have no power over any of the bounty of Allah, which is an expression for what they were given. The first view is preferable.

Ibn Mas'ud read "li-kay la ya'lama" (so that he may not know). Khattab ibn 'Abd Allah read "li-an ya'lama" (that he may know). 'Ikrimah read "li-ya'lama" (that he may know). It was also read "li-yalla" with the hamzah changed to a ya', and it was read with a fatha on the lam.

Abd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim, al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman transmitted, through the chains of Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: 'O 'Abd Allah!' I said: 'At your service, O Messenger of Allah,' three times. He said: 'Do you know which of the firmest handholds of Islam is the strongest?' I said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'The best of people is the one whose deeds are best when they comprehend their religion. O 'Abd Allah, do you know which of the people is most knowledgeable?' I said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'The most knowledgeable of people is the one who sees the truth most clearly when people differ, even if he falls short in deeds, even if he crawls on his backside. Those before us differed into seventy-two sects, of which three were saved and the rest perished: a sect which supported the kings and fought them in the cause of the religion of Allah and of Jesus, son of Mary; a sect which had no ability to support the kings, so they stayed among their people, calling them to the religion of Allah and the religion of Jesus, and the kings killed them and sawed them apart with saws; and a sect which had no ability to support the kings nor to remain among them, so they wandered in the mountains and lived there as monks. These are the ones of whom Allah said: ﴿But monasticism, they innovated it; We did not prescribe it for them, except seeking the pleasure of Allah. But they did not observe it with its proper observance. So We gave those of them who believed their reward; and many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾. Those who believed in Me and affirmed Me are the ones who believed, and ﴿many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾ are those who denied Me and disbelieved in Me.'"

Al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim, al-Tirmidhi in *Nawadir al-Usul*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: After 'Isa (Jesus), there were kings who altered the Torah and the Gospel. Among them were believers who read the Torah and the Gospel. It was said to their kings, "We find nothing more severe than the abuse that these people heap upon us. They recite, ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾, ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the wrongdoers﴾, ﴿those are the defiantly disobedient﴾, along with the faults they find in our deeds in their recitation. So summon them, and let them recite as we recite and believe as we believe." So the kings summoned them, gathered them, and offered them the choice of being killed or of abandoning the recitation of the Torah and the Gospel, except for what they had altered from them. They said, "What do you want from us with this? Leave us alone." A group among them said, "Build us a pillar, then raise us up to it, and give us something with which to lift up our food and drink, and we will not return to you." Another group said, "Leave us to travel through the earth and wander, and to eat what the wild beasts eat and drink what they drink. If you have power over us in your land, then kill us." Another group said, "Build us houses in the wilderness, and let us dig wells and cultivate herbs. Then we will not return to you nor pass by you." There was no tribe that did not have a close relative among them, and so they did this. Then Allah revealed: ﴿Monasticism, which they invented; We did not prescribe it for them, but they sought the pleasure of Allah, and they did not observe it with its proper observance﴾. Others, from among those who worshipped in polytheism, and when those who had passed away had died, said, "We will worship as so-and-so worshipped, and wander as so-and-so wandered, and take houses as so-and-so took houses," while they remained upon their polytheism and had no knowledge of the faith of those whom they followed. When the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent and only a few of them remained, the monk of the cell came down from his cell, the wanderer came back from his wandering, and the monk of the monastery came down from his monastery. They believed in him and affirmed him. Then Allah said: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah and believe in His Messenger; He will give you a double portion of His mercy﴾, meaning two rewards for their belief in 'Isa, their striving of themselves, and the Torah and the Gospel, and for their belief in Muhammad and their affirmation of him. ﴿And make for you a light by which you will walk﴾, meaning the Qur'an, and their following of the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ahmad, al-Hakim, al-Tirmidhi, Abu Ya'la, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* narrated from Anas that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Every nation has a monasticism, and the monasticism of this nation is jihad in the way of Allah."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari regarding His saying ﴿kiflayn﴾ (two portions, كِفْلَيْنِ) that he said: "Two-fold." And it is in the language of Abyssinia (Ethiopia).

Al-Firyabi, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Umar regarding His saying ﴿He will give you a double portion of His mercy﴾ that he said: "The *kifl* is three hundred and fifty parts of the mercy of Allah."
